rubric.text: Explains that text retrieved from memory enters the model's context and can be read as an instruction, so memory is an injection channel.
Explains that version checks and deep copies preserve content exactly and do not classify it as data or instruction.
Lists defenses: treat notes as untrusted data, delimit and label them, preserve provenance, and restrict which fields can influence control decisions.
Explains that authorization must be enforced at the tool boundary at execution time (allow-lists, scopes, approvals), because a prompt warning is a request and not an enforcement.
States that no single layer is sufficient, and that quarantine and monitoring are needed for records found to be suspicious.

questions.source: Shared notes are an input boundary
questions.prompt: A suspicious note is found in a shared store. Describe a quarantine mechanism as an alternative to deleting the note or leaving it active. Explain what the quarantine must do, what it preserves, what can still go wrong, and who must be responsible for it.

rubric.text: States that quarantine excludes the record from prompt construction while retaining it.
Explains that retention supports incident review: how the note got there, who wrote it, and which outputs it influenced.
Explains that the exclusion must be enforced in code that builds prompts and not by a label that nothing reads.
Identifies failure modes: a quarantine nobody reviews, false positives that block useful data, and copies or summaries of the note elsewhere.
Assigns an owner with a review process, an expiry or release path, and access controls on the quarantined content.

questions.source: Shared notes are an input boundary
questions.prompt: In a multi-agent system, one compromised worker writes a false claim into shared memory. Several other workers retrieve it and cite each other's outputs until the claim appears in many places. Explain how this can look like consensus, how to detect that it is one lineage, and what design choices reduce the spread.

rubric.text: Explains that repetition across workers can look like independent agreement even though the claim traces to one source.
Explains that each worker's retrieval and summarization copies the claim, so apparent support grows without new evidence.
Proposes detecting it by tracing each claim back through derivation links to the earliest record and counting independent origins.
Proposes tagging records with writer identity and run, and limiting which workers can write which keys.
Proposes requiring evidence beyond internal citations for high-impact claims, plus quarantine of the compromised writer's output for review.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.prompt: Write a role contract for a reviewer agent that checks whether claims C1 to C9 are supported by cited excerpts P1 to P4, and explain why each element of the contract matters. Contrast it with the instruction "Review the work."

rubric.text: Specifies inputs (the claims, the excerpts and the schema) and a narrowly defined task such as flagging claims the excerpts do not support.
Specifies tools and permissions, such as read-only access with no writes to memory, to limit harm.
Specifies an output format with claim ID, a three-valued verdict (supported, unsupported, cannot tell) and passage location, so results are checkable and comparable.
Specifies a budget (for example one pass) and an escalation path for uncertain items to a named person.
Explains that "Review the work" leaves scope, evidence standard, output and escalation undefined, so results are not comparable and failures are not attributable.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.prompt: A team of analysts will use an AI tool to synthesize evidence for a decision. Design a procedure that protects each analyst's independent initial judgment before any synthesis is shown. Explain what problem the sequencing prevents, how disagreement is preserved afterward, and how the record shows that the sequence was followed.

rubric.text: Explains that seeing a polished synthesis first anchors individual judgments and correlates them, shrinking the variety that group judgment depends on.
Specifies that each analyst writes and dates an initial judgment with reasons before seeing the synthesis.
Specifies deliberation afterward with sources visible, comparing initial judgments with the synthesis.
Specifies that disagreement and minority reasoning are preserved in the record and not averaged into smooth prose.
Specifies that timestamps or version history show the initial judgments predate the synthesis, and that model personas are not counted as people.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.prompt: A three-person team chooses a vendor. Each member holds some facts the others lack, and all hold a few facts in common. After a discussion that ends in a confident decision, the team writes up a summary from the shared notes. Explain the shared-information bias, why the summary may be missing facts that mattered, and what test or process would reveal this.

rubric.text: Defines the bias: groups tend to discuss information everyone already holds and under-pool information held by one member.
Explains that the best option may be identifiable only from the pooled private facts, a hidden-profile situation.
Explains that a summary of shared notes cannot contain facts nobody wrote down, and a smooth summary can flatten differences.
Proposes a test: mark each fact behind the decision as shared or held by one person, and check whether any decision-relevant fact was private.
Proposes process fixes such as individual written inputs before discussion, explicit prompts for unshared information, and recording dissent.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.prompt: A shared record "due_day" is at version 3 and says Friday. A researcher finds an updated official schedule that says Monday and has not yet written it. An explainer worker has read version 3 and is producing student-facing instructions that say Friday. Explain why this is not a version conflict, what the system needs to detect it, and describe the states and steps from discovery to resuming normal work.

rubric.text: Explains that no competing write has been attempted, so the version check cannot fire; the problem is new evidence that undermines work in progress.
Identifies the need for a dependency map linking outputs and tasks to the record versions they used.
Describes states such as challenged (evidence contradicts), paused (dependent tasks stop), reviewed (an owner evaluates evidence and scope), superseded (old record retired) and resumed.
States that a named person with authority interprets the evidence and that the new version is committed with provenance.
Explains that outputs already produced from version 3 must be regenerated or recalled, since correcting the record does not correct downstream copies.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.prompt: A reviewer commits version 4 of the "due_day" record, replacing Friday with Monday and adding the qualification "for section B only". Another worker, which read version 3, then submits "Monday" with expected version 3 and is rejected as stale. A teammate suggests the worker should simply reread and retry. Evaluate that suggestion and say what the worker should do.

rubric.text: Explains that the rejection means the worker's premise is out of date.
Explains that blind retry at version 4 would overwrite the reviewed value and lose the qualification.
Explains that a version check is not a merge algorithm and that content changes must be compared.
States that the worker should reread, compare what changed in meaning, and either withdraw or submit a new proposal for review.
Says the original proposal should be preserved with evidence for the reviewer, and that swallowing the exception and logging success would hide a lost proposal.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.prompt: Two agents both read an order as "pending" and each call a payment API to charge 40 dollars. Both charges succeed. Afterward one agent's update to shared memory is rejected as stale. Explain why the rejection does not fix the problem, what an idempotency key is, how to choose one, and what mistakes in key design weaken it.

rubric.text: Explains that memory writes and external actions are separate effects, so rejecting a memory update does not reverse a charge that has been made.
Defines an idempotency key as an identifier sent with a request so the receiver treats repeats of the same logical operation as one.
Explains that the key should identify the logical operation (for example order and purpose), not each attempt, so retries and parallel duplicates share it.
Gives key-design mistakes: a random key per attempt, a key that includes a timestamp, or a key scoped too broadly so distinct legitimate actions are blocked.
Explains that coordination must happen at the action boundary, such as claiming the work item atomically before acting, and that the memory store's version check does not protect external systems.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.prompt: A company stores full prompts and tool results from agent runs to support incident reviews. Some contain customer data. Discuss the tension between replay and privacy, what policy decisions are required, and how redaction can go wrong.

rubric.text: Explains that complete traces help reconstruct why a decision occurred, while they may hold personal or sensitive data.
Lists policy decisions: what is stored, for how long, who can read it, and how deletion works.
Explains that replacing every value with a generic mask can leave a trace that no longer shows why a decision occurred.
Describes better redaction that preserves structure, such as consistent pseudonyms or field-level minimization.
Says the trace store needs access controls, audit logging and retention limits equal to those of the primary data, and that policy should be tested with actual deletion and access checks.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.prompt: An engineer removes a user's record from an in-memory dictionary that backs an agent's memory and reports "the user's data has been deleted." Explain what this evidence supports and what it does not, list places copies may remain, and describe how a deletion test and report should be worded.

rubric.text: States that the evidence supports "removed from this dictionary" in this process at this time.
Lists other places copies may live: logs, prompt and tool-result traces, backups, replicas, caches and other processes.
Notes that derived data such as summaries, embeddings or entries in other records are separate and need their own deletion.
Describes a test that checks each location and reports which were checked and which were not.
Gives careful wording, such as "deleted from X and Y; not verified for Z", rather than a blanket claim of deletion everywhere.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.prompt: After an incident in a multi-agent system, a team must write a replay of what happened. Logs show a worker read a record "sometime before version 4 was committed" but did not save which version was returned. An assistant offers to write the timeline from the fragments. Describe what the replay should contain, how to handle the gap, and the risk of letting a language model reconstruct the story.

rubric.text: Lists contents: which version each worker read, which output depended on it, what new evidence challenged it, and who had authority to interpret it.
Includes which external effects had already occurred and whether they were reversible, and which artifacts were invalidated or left unresolved.
Says that the unknown version should be recorded as unknown, and not filled in with a likely value.
Explains that language models write coherent narratives from fragments, including fragments that do not fit, so fluency can hide gaps and invented links.
Says the replay should state the checks that allowed work to resume and which events are supported by logs versus inference.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.prompt: Design the record format and access rules for a shared memory used by agents that draft public-facing instructions. Address how stored facts should be presented to a model, how proposed facts differ from accepted ones, which fields a record might carry, and what each worker is allowed to read.

rubric.text: States that stored values are rendered as quoted claims with provenance in a data section, not placed in the instruction channel.
Separates proposed from accepted facts, for example a proposal queue, review by a person or process, and commit against an expected version.
Proposes fields such as version, value, source identifier, supporting excerpt, observed-at, valid-until, verification status, supersedes pointer and sensitivity label.
Notes that each added field needs rules for who may set it and what empty values mean.
Applies reads by purpose: a worker writing public instructions receives only public, current, accepted fields.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.prompt: A team's tests for a version-checked store pass. The tests check the default for a missing key, the version returned by a first write, rejection of a stale write, and rejection of a blank source. Describe three faulty implementations that would still pass these tests, explain why, and say what further tests would catch each.

rubric.text: Describes a store whose read returns the stored object (aliasing) and explains that none of the four tests mutates a returned value.
Describes a store that checks the version outside the lock or atomic section and explains that one-at-a-time tests cannot interleave.
Describes a coordinator that retries a rejected write at the fresh version, and explains that the stale-write test still sees the first rejection.
Gives tests for each: mutate-then-reread; a threaded stress test; a test that the proposal is preserved and a reviewer decision is required.
States that passing tests establish only the behaviors tested, and untested properties should be listed as not checked.

questions.source: Two workers, one key
questions.prompt: A test run applies three writes in order to a version-checked store: "blue" at expected version 0 is accepted; "red" at expected 1 is accepted; "blue" at expected 1 is rejected. Say what this sequential run does and does not show about the store, and what you would add to support stronger claims about concurrent use.

rubric.text: States that the run shows deterministic version behavior: accepts at matching versions and rejects stale ones.
States that it shows nothing about behavior under simultaneous writers, since the calls never overlap.
Notes that the rejection reflects version order only, not which of the values is correct.
Proposes concurrent tests with threads or processes, repeated many times, plus a design argument about atomicity.
Says that tests can show a fault but silence does not prove its absence, so claims about concurrency should be stated narrowly.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.prompt: Compare two entries in a risk plan for a shared agent memory. Entry X: "Monitor for stale memory." Entry Y: "On a stale-version exception for a record used by an active task, pause dependent actions, preserve both proposals, notify the decision owner, and resume only after a reviewed version is committed." Explain why Y is operational and X is not, and write the table row you would add for each failure of your choice.

rubric.text: Identifies in Y a trigger, a response, an owner and a recovery condition, each of which can be tested.
Explains that X names no trigger, action, owner or success condition, so nobody can tell whether it was done.
Writes a full row for a chosen failure (for example duplicate actions or prompt injection) with control, detection evidence and residual risk.
Explains that each control has its own failure mode, such as a quarantine nobody reviews or an idempotency key scoped wrongly.
Explains that detection and recovery need separate tests, including the path in which the reviewer rejects the change.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.prompt: A team has built a workflow in which a stale-write conflict pauses a dependent task, a reviewer examines the competing proposals, and a reviewed version is committed before the task resumes. Design the tests that show this recovery works. Include the case in which the reviewer rejects the change, and explain why a workflow that always accepts the newest proposal is not protected by having a review step.

rubric.text: Describes a test that creates the stale conflict and checks that the dependent task is paused and no dependent action runs.
Checks that both proposals and their evidence are preserved for the reviewer.
Checks that after the reviewed version is committed the task rereads the record before resuming.
Describes the reject path: the reviewer rejects with a recorded reason and the original record stays in force, with the task resuming on the unchanged value or remaining blocked per policy.
Explains that always committing the newest proposal is last-writer-wins behind a ceremony, because the decision does not depend on the reviewer's judgment.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.prompt: An engineer finishes a risk review of a shared agent memory and must sign it. Describe what a responsible sign-off statement contains, why the "not checked" part matters most, and why a statement drafted by an AI assistant tends to be weak on exactly that point. Give three concrete examples of items that might appear under "not checked".

rubric.text: States that a sign-off says what was checked and how, what was not checked, and what is not being claimed.
Explains that the not-checked list tells readers how far to rely on the review, and that an omission looks like coverage.
Explains that an assistant knows only what it was given and has no record of work the engineer did not do, so it tends to produce fluent, complete-sounding claims.
Gives three plausible items, such as behavior under real concurrent load, other processes and restarts, deletion in backups, or whether any stored source is true.

States that if the evidence does not support signing, withholding is an honest outcome, and a statement that claims more than the record supports repeats the failure of an unchecked, official-looking record.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.prompt: An agent writes notes into a shared channel. On later runs it reads the channel and treats its earlier notes as outside evidence, sometimes as if another agent had written them. Explain why this is a problem for confirmation counting, how to detect it, and what interaction-level checks should supplement testing each agent alone.

rubric.text: Explains that reading back one's own output adds no new information, so counting it as confirmation is double counting.
Explains that a model may fail to recognize its earlier messages as its own when they appear in a shared channel.
Proposes tagging each record with writer identity and run, and scanning claims for evidence the same worker authored.
States that such cases count as zero confirmations in the evidence tally.
Proposes interaction-level checks: which workers may write and read which keys, handoff validation against sources, and tracing lineage across workers.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.prompt: Three streams of analysis in a project all point to the same site, and a fourth analysis on labor costs is recorded but changes nothing in the final recommendation. A reviewer is asked how to check the project's joints and not only its sections. Explain how to treat the idle fourth analysis, why agreement between the first three may be less informative than it seems, and how to avoid inventing reasons to reopen decisions.

rubric.text: Explains that agreement counts as confirmation only if the routes are independent, and shared assumptions or inputs can produce convergence.
Says an idle finding should be examined: either explained as irrelevant with a reason, or treated as a reason to reopen an earlier decision.
Explains that checking each section alone misses contradictions at the joints between sections.
Gives a practical check, such as scanning for evidence that arrived and moved nothing, and asking who owns reopening the decision.
Warns against creating a reopening event just to complete an exercise, because that adds a fabricated record.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.prompt: A long-running agent will exceed its context window. Compare three techniques for handling that: compaction of the conversation into a summary, structured note-taking to storage outside the context window, and delegation to sub-agents that return condensed results. Discuss strengths, risks, and when you would use each.

rubric.text: Describes compaction: summarizing the history near the limit and continuing with the summary; strength is continuity, risk is loss or distortion of detail.
Describes structured note-taking: the agent writes notes to external storage and retrieves them later; strength is persistence, risk is stale or wrong notes.
Describes sub-agents: each explores with its own context and returns a condensed result; strength is focus and parallelism, risk is token cost and lossy handoffs.
Notes that long contexts can degrade attention, so context is a finite resource to be curated rather than filled.
Gives selection guidance, such as compaction for continuous dialogue, notes for milestones and decisions, and sub-agents for breadth-first independent exploration.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.prompt: An orchestrator agent uses 30,000 tokens. It spawns five parallel sub-agents that each use 40,000 tokens. A single agent doing the same task alone would use 90,000 tokens. Compute the total for the multi-agent design and compare. Then discuss when the added cost is justified and what the orchestrator still has to check.

rubric.text: Computes 30,000 + 5 x 40,000 = 230,000 tokens for the multi-agent design.
Compares: it is about 2.6 times the single agent's 90,000 tokens, so it costs more in tokens.
Explains that parallelism can reduce wall-clock time, not total work, and that breadth-first tasks with independent subtasks benefit most.
Explains that tasks with tightly dependent steps or heavy shared context suit parallel sub-agents poorly.
States that the orchestrator must verify sub-agent outputs and handoffs, since same-model workers can share errors.

questions.source: Memory is stored state, not recollection
questions.prompt: Agent designers often borrow terms from cognitive psychology: working memory, episodic memory, semantic memory and procedural memory. Define each as applied to an LLM agent and give a concrete example of how an agent could implement each. Then explain one risk shared by all external stored memories.

rubric.text: Defines working or short-term memory as the contents of the context window for the current task.
Defines episodic memory as records of specific past events or interactions, for example logs of earlier sessions retrieved by similarity.
Defines semantic memory as general facts independent of an episode, for example a knowledge base or user profile.
Defines procedural memory as how-to knowledge, for example stored instructions, skills or learned routines.
Identifies a shared risk: stored content can be stale, wrong or poisoned, and nothing about retrieval verifies it.

questions.source: Memory is stored state, not recollection
questions.prompt: An agent ranks memories by a weighted sum of recency, importance and relevance, each scored from 0 to 1. Memory M1 scores recency 0.9, importance 0.2, relevance 0.5. Memory M2 scores recency 0.3, importance 0.9, relevance 0.8. Compute the totals for equal weights, and for weights of 5, 1 and 1 on recency, importance and relevance respectively. Discuss what the weights represent and what the scores do not guarantee.

rubric.text: Computes the equal-weight totals: M1 = 1.6 and M2 = 2.0, so M2 ranks higher.
Computes the weighted totals: M1 = 5.2 and M2 = 3.2, so M1 ranks higher.
Explains that the ranking flips because weights encode a design choice about what matters most.
Explains that tuning weights should be done against evaluation on real retrieval tasks and not guessed.
States that high scores indicate likely usefulness, not correctness, and a retrieved memory can still be stale or false.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes
questions.prompt: An agent replaces its history with a new summary after every step, discarding the earlier summary and raw records. Analyze the risks of this design and propose an alternative that keeps the benefits of summarizing.

rubric.text: Explains that each summary is built from the previous one, so information dropped early is unrecoverable.
Explains that errors or distortions in early summaries propagate into later ones.
Explains that without raw records nobody can audit the summary against what actually happened.
Notes that summarization can drop qualifiers, over-generalize or introduce unsupported statements.
Proposes keeping raw records and deriving summaries from them, labeling summaries as derived, and periodically checking them against the originals.

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.prompt: Two workers submit conflicting values for the same record. Compare four resolution policies: last-writer-wins, first-writer-wins, compare-and-set with rejection of stale writes, and an automatic merge rule. Explain the risks of each and which questions none of them answers.

rubric.text: States that last-writer-wins silently discards the earlier value whatever its merit.
States that first-writer-wins preserves arrival order and also does not test truth.
States that compare-and-set detects stale premises and forces the loser to reconsider, without choosing a value.
States that automatic merge can combine edits mechanically, may produce a value neither source supports, and works only where merge semantics are well defined.
States that none of them answers which value is true, who is authorized to decide, or what depends on the old value.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.prompt: A shared record can be overwritten in place, or kept as a chain of versions in which each version points to the one it supersedes. Discuss the benefits and costs of each approach for an agent system that must be audited after incidents.

rubric.text: States that a versioned chain lets a reviewer reconstruct what a worker read at a given time.
States that a supersedes pointer records that a value was replaced, not that it was wrong.
States that in-place overwriting loses history and makes replay and error analysis harder.
Identifies costs of keeping history: storage, privacy and retention obligations, and the need to make readers see only the current version by default.
Proposes policy: retain history for a defined period with access controls, and delete or minimize on a schedule or request, documenting what is retained.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.prompt: A team adds a field "verification" to every stored record with values such as "unverified" and "human-reviewed". In the first implementation any worker can set the field on write. Critique this design and propose how to make the field meaningful.

rubric.text: Identifies that a worker setting its own record's status is self-attestation and not verification.
Explains that valid-looking strings show nothing about whether a review took place.
Proposes restricting who can set the field to a defined reviewer role and recording who set it and when.
Proposes tying the status to evidence, such as a link to the reviewed source and the reviewed version, and invalidating it when the value changes.
Explains that every added field creates validation questions, and a field that code and policy do not enforce gives only the appearance of rigor.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.prompt: A team of agents shares a store. Describe how to document which workers may write and read which keys, what questions that documentation lets reviewers answer, and why it complements, and does not replace, record-level provenance.

rubric.text: Describes a matrix or policy listing each worker with its permitted write keys and read keys.
Explains that least-privilege writes limit the damage a faulty or compromised worker can do.
Explains that read restrictions limit what sensitive or low-trust data a worker can see and act on.
Explains that the matrix lets a reviewer check whether a worker's evidence includes something it wrote itself, and which workers could have influenced a claim.
Explains that provenance records what actually happened to a particular claim, while permissions describe what was allowed, so both are needed.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.prompt: A shared store holds 200 notes, 10 of which are wrong. A reviewer checks 20 notes chosen uniformly at random without replacement. The chance that the sample contains none of the wrong notes is about 0.34; with a sample of 40 it falls to about 0.10. Interpret these numbers, explain what a clean sample does and does not allow you to claim, and describe how you would choose a sampling plan.

rubric.text: Interprets 0.34 as the chance the reviewer would see no wrong note in 20 and therefore feel falsely reassured, so detection probability is about 0.66.
Interprets the 40-note sample: miss probability about 0.10 and detection about 0.90, showing larger samples lower the miss chance.
States that a clean sample does not prove the store has no wrong notes.
States that the supportable claim is limited to the sample, its size and selection method.
Describes sampling choices: random selection, stratifying by risk or by writer, sampling more where consequences are higher, and deciding in advance what miss rate is acceptable.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.prompt: A writer agent produces a wrong note 5 percent of the time. One reviewer catches 80 percent of wrong notes. Two other reviewers, if their misses are independent, each catch 70 percent. Compute the share of all notes that are wrong and pass the single 80 percent reviewer, and the share of wrong notes missed by both independent 70 percent reviewers. Then explain what happens if the two reviewers are the same model with the same prompt, and how to get useful diversity.

rubric.text: Computes 0.05 x 0.2 = 0.01, so 1 percent of all notes are wrong and pass the single reviewer.
Computes 0.3 x 0.3 = 0.09, so 9 percent of wrong notes are missed by both independent reviewers.
Explains that same-model, same-prompt reviewers have correlated misses, so their joint miss rate is far above 9 percent and may be near 30 percent.
Explains that a reviewer that sees the writer's conclusion first may anchor on it and catch less.
Proposes diversity: different information sources or methods, a different model or deterministic checks, blind review, and a human for high-stakes items.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: A test log shows that a write raised "Stale memory version", that another write returned version 5, and that a later read returned "red". A draft report says "The store rejected the bad update, verified the new value of red, and resolved the dispute between workers." Rewrite the claim so that every verb is supported by the log, and explain what each overclaim confused.

rubric.text: Supports "rejected" with the observed exception, and notes it describes a refused write, not a judgment about the update's quality.
Supports "committed" or "accepted as version 5" for the second write.
Explains that "verified the new value" overclaims, because verification requires a criterion and evidence the log lacks.
Explains that "resolved the dispute" overclaims, because rejecting one write leaves the question of which value is right open.

Gives a rewrite such as "One write was rejected as stale; another was committed as version 5; a read returned red; correctness of red was not checked," and names the conflations (newer and truer, rejected and resolved, committed and verified).

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.prompt: A store holds booking state for two rooms under a single key, with one version counter. Workers update the rooms independently. Discuss the problems with this design, the problems with splitting it into one key per room, and how to choose the granularity of the thing one version covers.

rubric.text: Explains that a single key makes unrelated updates conflict, producing false conflicts and needless retries.
Explains that splitting by room removes false conflicts for independent updates.
Explains that after splitting, a decision depending on both rooms is no longer covered by one version, so a change in one input is invisible to the other's counter.
Describes mitigations: recording input versions with dependent decisions, or a transaction or covering version for multi-key decisions.
States the principle: choose the version boundary to match the units of consistency the application needs, and decide it before workers run.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.prompt: A reviewer agent is given a budget of one pass and an instruction to send any item it cannot judge to a named person. Explain why budgets and escalation paths should be designed in advance for autonomous workers, what can go wrong without them, and what the reviewer should return when it runs out of budget.

rubric.text: Explains that a budget limits cost and the damage of loops, drift or runaway retries.
Explains that unbounded autonomy makes it unclear who decided what or who is accountable.
Explains that an escalation route chosen in advance turns uncertainty into a routed question instead of a guess.
Describes failure modes without them: endless retries, silent guessing, or confident verdicts on items the worker could not assess.
States that on budget exhaustion the worker should return an explicit "cannot tell" or partial result with what remains unchecked, not a result presented as complete or verified.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.prompt: A developer asks an assistant for deliberately wrong versions of a memory store that still pass the existing tests, such as one that returns a reference to the stored list or one that retries rejected writes at the fresh version. Explain what the exercise measures, how to interpret the results, and why the tests should not be written only by the source of the implementation.

rubric.text: Identifies the technique as seeding plausible faults, akin to mutation testing, to measure whether tests detect them.
Explains that a faulty version that passes shows the tests are too weak for that fault.
Explains that a faulty version that fails shows the test is sensitive to that fault.
States that passing tests on the correct implementation do not prove the absence of other faults.
Explains that tests authored by the same source as the implementation share its assumptions and blind spots, so independent test authorship, or a human-written baseline, adds value.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.prompt: A learner is told to write their own simple memory store before looking at a reference implementation, and to write down dated predictions before running it. Explain the learning and engineering reasons for these steps, and what the learner should do with a prediction that turns out wrong.

rubric.text: Explains that predictions made before the result guard against hindsight bias.
Explains that a mismatch between prediction and result exposes an error in the learner's mental model.
Says the original predictions should be kept unedited so the gap stays visible.
Explains that building a baseline first gives an object to compare an AI-generated version against and the understanding to judge it.
Explains that one cannot audit a mechanism one has never implemented or broken, so the baseline supports verification.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: An agent system flags a conflict between two proposals for the same record. An AI assistant can summarize the proposals and evidence. Describe which parts of resolving the conflict an assistant can do well, which parts need a named accountable person, and how to record the decision so that it can later be reviewed.

rubric.text: Says the assistant can lay out both proposals and their evidence, retrieve sources, and flag overlaps or gaps.
Says the assistant can summarize disagreement without flattening it, if the originals are kept.
Says a named person should decide, since the decision carries stakes, local knowledge and accountability that a summary cannot hold.
Says the decision should be one of commit, reject with a reason, or leave unresolved, and that unresolved is a legitimate recorded state.
Says the record should include the decision, the person, the date, the evidence considered and the versions involved.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.prompt: Record 1 says an assignment closes Friday. A new official source says Monday. In a sequential workflow, a plan was written from Record 1 and each later step just built on it. Explain the difference between running a project's parts strictly in order and then summarizing, and managing the parts together so that a finding in one can reopen an earlier decision, using this example. Describe the events that should reopen earlier decisions.

rubric.text: Describes the in-order approach: parts are completed one after another and then summarized, so later findings do not reach back to change earlier decisions.
Describes the integrated approach: parts are held together so a finding in one can reopen another.
Applies it: the Monday source should reopen the decision that depended on Friday and everything built on it.
Lists concrete reopening events, such as a newer source, a reviewer's correction, a failed spot check, or a stale-version exception on a key an active task read.
Says each event needs an owner and a resume condition, written down before work starts, so that a plan does not stay in force after its evidence is gone.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.prompt: An assistant should decide what to remember about users over time. Some stored facts will become outdated, some will be wrong, and some are sensitive. Propose a memory write and update policy: what to store, how to handle changed facts, how to treat uncertainty and sensitivity, and how users can inspect and correct memory.

rubric.text: Proposes selective writing: store only facts needed for the task, with a defined purpose, instead of keeping everything.
Proposes recording source, time and confidence with each fact, and marking inferred facts separately from stated ones.
Proposes a policy for changed facts: supersede with history or confirm with the user, rather than silently overwriting.
Proposes sensitivity handling: minimization, access limits, retention limits and no storage of data the user declined to share.
Proposes user-facing inspection, correction and deletion, and expiry or re-confirmation of facts likely to go stale.

questions.source: Shared notes are an input boundary
questions.prompt: An attacker gets a false instruction-like note into an agent's long-term memory through a web page the agent summarized. The note affects the agent's behavior in later sessions. Explain why persistence makes this worse than a one-off prompt injection, how you would detect the planted memory, and how you would recover.

rubric.text: Explains that persistent memory carries the injected text into many later sessions and can be retrieved without the original web page being present.
Explains that later reads treat it as the agent's own memory, so its low-trust origin is lost unless provenance is stored.
Describes detection: provenance and write-origin audit, scanning for instruction-like text in records, and monitoring tool calls that deviate from policy.
Describes recovery: quarantine or remove the record, trace and review outputs and actions that used it, and notify affected owners.
Describes prevention: treat retrieved notes as untrusted data, restrict what may be written to memory from untrusted sources, and enforce authorization at the tool boundary.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.prompt: A reviewer is shown a proposal to write a file named report.md. She reads the supporting evidence and clicks Approve, and the system stores a record containing "approved", her name and a timestamp. Later, before the write happens, the target of the proposal is changed to a different path. Explain how the stored approval can still appear valid even though the thing it approved no longer exists, and describe the technical measure that prevents this.

rubric.text: Identifies that the record attests only that someone said yes, at a time, under a name; none of those three facts identifies what was approved.
Explains that after the target changed, the old yes would be presented as permission for an action the reviewer never saw.
Proposes binding the decision to the exact proposal content, for example a hash of a canonical serialization of the whole proposal, stored with the decision.
States that the fingerprint must be recomputed from the proposal about to execute and compared with the stored value at the point of the effect.
Explains that a mismatch must send the changed proposal back to review as a new decision, and notes that content binding does not show who approved or that anyone read it.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.prompt: An agent harness asks a human "Allow the agent to run this command?" and shows only the command name and two buttons. Explain what information a reviewer needs before a yes can be meaningful, and why each item is needed.

rubric.text: Names the specific action to be performed, stated precisely enough to show what operation will occur.
Names the resolved target (path, account, environment or recipient) rather than a friendly label that could refer to several objects.
Requires a reason that ties the action to the user's task, because capability or permission alone does not show the action is wanted.
Requires the anticipated effects, including external and irreversible ones, and the evidence supporting the decision to proceed, as references that can be checked.
Requires an honest statement of how the action could be undone, including when recovery is partial or impossible, and explains that this shifts the burden from the reviewer to the request.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an approval request that is structurally complete and one that is substantively adequate. Give a concrete example of a request that is complete but inadequate, and describe which mechanisms can catch each kind of problem.

rubric.text: Defines structural completeness as the required fields being present and well formed, which a schema or validator can check mechanically.
Defines substantive adequacy as the content being specific, accurate, and credible for the action, which presence checks cannot judge.
Gives a valid example, such as evidence that reads only "looks good" or effects listed as "none" for a destructive action, that passes a presence check.
Describes mechanisms for substantive problems: reviewer judgment, links to checkable artifacts, domain-expert review, and graders whose scores are treated as evidence rather than decisions.
States that a passing validator should be reported as a structural result and not as an assessment of the proposal's quality or safety.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.prompt: An agent requests approval to "update the shared config". Explain why a display name or relative path is an inadequate description of the target in an approval request, and describe what the request should contain instead.

rubric.text: Explains that one name can refer to several objects, such as files in different directories or in different environments.
Gives examples of how the real target can differ from the displayed one, such as symbolic links, relative paths, or ".." segments.
States that the request should show a resolved identity, such as the canonical absolute path, account, environment, or recipient.
Notes that the consequential difference (for example, a file shared with other teams or a production system) is often exactly what the friendly name hides.
Explains that the reviewer cannot be expected to discover this unaided, so the interface and request format must surface it.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: In an automated review pipeline for agent actions, define evaluation and authorization, explain why they should be kept distinct, and say what a test suite, a policy checker, and a model-based grader can and cannot decide.

rubric.text: Defines evaluation as producing evidence about what happened or could happen and how well a proposal meets stated criteria.
Defines authorization as a decision by a responsible person or policy that the action may proceed; it spends the evidence evaluation produced.
Explains that merging the two on one screen makes a passing score look like permission and hides who made the decision.
States that a test suite evaluates selected behaviors but cannot decide whether a destructive change is worth making.
States that a policy checker flags rule violations but cannot judge exceptions, and that a model grader's score is evidence with its own failure modes and not a decision.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: A team watches an agent attempt ten tasks, then writes evaluation cases around what it did and adjusts expected answers until all ten pass. Explain what is wrong with this process and describe the order of work that keeps an evaluation capable of finding problems.

rubric.text: Identifies that the criteria were chosen after seeing the outputs, so the passing result records accommodation to the observed behavior.
Explains that such an evaluation could not have failed, so a pass tells the reader little about the system.
Recommends deciding in advance what outcomes would count as evidence against the proposal, before looking at evidence in its favor.
Recommends including cases chosen to embarrass the system: boundary conditions, refusal cases, and structurally complete but weak inputs.
Recommends recording expected outcomes before running, and documenting any later change to an expectation with its reason.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: An agent is asked to close inactive accounts. The database tool logged a single successful UPDATE with "42 rows affected", but the agent's final message says it closed 99 accounts. Distinguish trace evidence, narration, and outcome evidence, and design an independent check that could contradict the agent's claim.

rubric.text: Defines trace evidence as the record of what commands or calls were made and what they returned.
Defines narration as the agent's own statement of what happened, which can be fluent and wrong.
Defines outcome evidence as an observation of the resulting state of the system, separate from the agent's actions and statements.
Designs a post-action check, such as an independent query counting accounts in the closed state before and after, compared with the expected number.
Explains what the check establishes and its scope, noting that it covers only the state it queries and not other side effects.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: A team reports that a file-writing agent "passed 20 of 20 evaluation cases", where every case wrote an ordinary text file into an empty directory. Explain what the result does and does not show, and what the team should record so that readers can interpret it.

rubric.text: Explains that the result shows the agent handled the kinds of situations the cases covered.
Lists situations left untested, such as symbolic links, permission errors, concurrent changes, path traversal, existing files, or private data.
States that a pass count cannot be interpreted without knowing which cases ran and why they represent the intended use.
Recommends recording exclusions beside the result, so that a reader can see where the evidence stops.
Recommends adding cases designed to expose boundary and refusal behavior rather than more cases of the same kind.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: An evaluation set for an agent that decides whether to carry out file operations has 30 cases whose correct behavior is to proceed and 10 whose correct behavior is to refuse. Calculate the score an always-proceed agent and an always-refuse agent would each receive, and explain what this shows about designing and reporting such evaluations.

rubric.text: Computes the always-proceed agent's accuracy as 30 of 40, or 75%.
Computes the always-refuse agent's accuracy as 10 of 40, or 25%.
Explains that a single accuracy figure can make a useless policy look respectable, and that the result depends on the mix of cases.
Recommends reporting the rate for each class of case separately (for example, correct proceeds and correct refusals).
Explains that a set with no should-refuse cases cannot distinguish a careful agent from an indiscriminate one.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: After a redesign of its approval screen, a team celebrates that median time to approval fell sharply. Explain why optimizing one such metric can make an approval process worse, name at least four measurements that can pull against each other, and describe how results should be reported.

rubric.text: Explains that time to approval can fall because reviewers click reflexively or because the screen hides detail, not because review became more efficient.
Names task success as one measure that may rise while others worsen.
Names the rate of invalid or later-reversed actions as a measure of whether decisions were well informed.
Names reviewer burden and refusal or deferral rates as further measures that can move in opposing directions.
Recommends reporting a portfolio of measures together, including errors and deferrals, and not a single celebratory number.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: A team uses a language model to grade free-text rollback plans against a rubric. Describe the failure modes of this approach, how the team should calibrate it, and how it should be combined with other kinds of checks.

rubric.text: Identifies that fluent, detailed prose can score well while omitting an irreversible side effect or being factually wrong.
Identifies that graders sharing a prompt, rubric assumption, or source error can agree and still be wrong together, so agreement is not independent confirmation.
Recommends calibrating the grader against human-labeled examples and analyzing its failures before trusting its scores.
Recommends pairing it with deterministic checks wherever the property can be checked mechanically.
Recommends human review proportional to the stakes, and treating the grader's output as evidence for that review rather than as the decision.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: A prototype approval gate passes all 8 of 8 evaluation cases. Assuming the cases were independent random draws from real usage, compute the approximate 95% upper confidence bound on the true failure rate (using 1 - 0.05^(1/8), and the "rule of three" shortcut 3/n), and explain what the team can and cannot responsibly claim.

rubric.text: Computes the exact bound as about 31% (1 - 0.05^(1/8) = 0.312).
Computes the rule-of-three approximation as 3/8, or about 37.5%, and notes it is a rough upper estimate.
Explains that zero failures in a small sample leaves a wide range of plausible true failure rates.
Explains that hand-picked cases are not a random sample and so do not support a population reliability figure at all.
Recommends reporting the cases and what they covered and excluded rather than a reliability percentage.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: An agent succeeds on a task independently with probability 0.9 on each attempt, and is evaluated with 5 trials per task. Compute the probability of at least one success and the probability that all five trials succeed, and explain which measure matters for a destructive action that must be right every time and which for a task where failures can simply be retried.

rubric.text: Computes the probability of at least one success as 1 - 0.1^5 = 0.99999.
Computes the probability of all five succeeding as 0.9^5, about 0.59.
Explains that the gap between the two shows how much a single headline number can hide about consistency.
States that for an action that causes harm when it fails, the all-trials (consistency) measure is the relevant one.
States that for cheaply retried tasks with verifiable results, the at-least-one measure can be appropriate, and that single trials are not enough for a nondeterministic system.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: During an evaluation run, one case produces a result different from the expected outcome written down beforehand. Describe how a team should handle the discrepancy and why simply editing the expectation is a problem.

rubric.text: States that the discrepancy may come from the implementation, the test's expectation, or the original requirement.
Recommends investigating each possibility rather than assuming the implementation is at fault.
Explains that silently editing the expectation to match the output turns the evaluation into accommodation.
Recommends recording any change to an expectation or requirement, with the reason and the date.
Notes that a surprising result, harmless or not, should feed into the next version of the evaluation set.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: Explain why an evaluation of an agent should keep full transcripts and tool traces yet grade outcomes, and say what a useful record for each evaluation case contains.

rubric.text: Explains that transcripts and traces show what the agent said and did, which helps diagnose failures.
Explains that outcomes are the resulting state of the world, and an agent can claim success without that state having changed.
States that the record should contain the task input and the expected behavior, written in advance.
States that the record should contain the actual output, the checker used, and the rationale for any discrepancy.
Explains that a single aggregate score discards the trace of what failed, which is what a reviewer most needs to see.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.prompt: Two services each build the same approval proposal as a Python dictionary, inserting the keys in different orders, and each hashes the output of json.dumps with SHA-256. The digests differ. Explain why serialization must be canonical before hashing, which choices make Python's output canonical for this purpose, and what additional problems remain if the services are written in different languages.

rubric.text: Explains that a hash operates on bytes, and equivalent data serialized differently produces different bytes and so different digests.
Identifies that dictionary insertion order leaks into the output, although JSON objects have no meaningful key order.
Names sorting the keys as the fix for order, and fixed separators (no optional whitespace) and a fixed encoding such as UTF-8 as fixes for formatting.
Names cross-language problems such as number formatting (1 versus 1.0), Unicode normalization, string escaping, and duplicate keys.
Recommends a written canonicalization specification (such as RFC 8785) shared by both services, and notes that the canonical form decides what counts as the same proposal.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.prompt: A system stores a SHA-256 digest of each approval request in a log and treats it as proof of approval. Explain what a digest of a proposal does establish, what it does not establish, and which additional mechanisms would be needed to establish the rest.

rubric.text: States that a digest establishes content identity: a changed proposal produces a different digest, so a stored value detects modification.
States that a digest does not provide secrecy, since anyone who has or can guess the content can compute it and compare.
States that a digest does not establish who produced the record, because no secret is involved in computing it.
States that it does not show that a person read or understood the proposal, or had authority to approve it.
Names mechanisms for the rest: digital signatures or keyed MACs for authenticity, authenticated sessions or credentials for identity, an authority registry, and processes for review quality.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.prompt: Approval gates must decide what counts as "the same proposal". Discuss the difference between comparing exact bytes and comparing meaning, using path spellings and symbolic links as examples, and explain the trade-off between false rejections and false acceptances.

rubric.text: Explains that fingerprinting a string treats two spellings of the same file, such as "./report.md" and "report.md", as different proposals.
Explains that an identical string can refer to a different object later, for example when a symbolic link is repointed or a mutable name is reassigned.
Recommends binding resolved identifiers, immutable versions, or content hashes of the object in high-stakes cases.
Explains that false rejections (re-asking over irrelevant differences) cost reviewer attention and breed fatigue.

Explains that false acceptances (reusing approval for a consequentially different action) defeat the approval gate, so the canonical form should erase noise but preserve every consequential difference.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.prompt: A Python gate rejects a proposal if `not proposal.get(field)` is true for any of six required fields. Explain which inputs this check rejects and accepts, why that is not a check of meaning, and how the validation could be strengthened and what limits would remain.

rubric.text: States that falsey values such as empty strings, empty lists, None, 0 and False are rejected.
States that any non-empty string is accepted, including whitespace only, "0", "n/a", or fluent but meaningless text.
Explains that the check tests presence and form, not whether the content is adequate for the action.
Suggests stricter checks: required types, trimmed non-empty strings, length or format limits, and references to artifacts that can be resolved.
States that even strict validation cannot judge adequacy or credibility, which still need reviewer judgment.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.prompt: A review interface and a backend both receive the same JSON text, {"target":"report.md","target":"/etc/passwd"}. The interface parser keeps the first value of a repeated key and the backend parser keeps the last. Explain what goes wrong, why hashing the text does not fix it, and how to prevent the problem.

rubric.text: Explains that the reviewer sees one target while the executor acts on another although both processed identical bytes.
Names this as a parser differential: different parsers resolve duplicate keys differently, and the standard leaves this behavior unspecified.
Explains that a digest of the raw text only shows the bytes are unchanged, not that the two sides interpret them alike.
Recommends rejecting documents with duplicate keys at ingestion with a strict parser.
Recommends parsing once, then fingerprinting and executing the same parsed canonical object, so the reviewer sees what runs.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.prompt: Describe in prose the conditions under which a stored decision record should authorize a single attempt at an action, and explain why each condition exists.

rubric.text: States that the decision must be an explicit, strictly typed approval, not merely a truthy value, because loosely typed values such as "no" can evaluate as true.
States that the approver must be identified, ideally by an authenticated identity with authority for this action, not just a nonblank string.
States that the recorded fingerprint must equal a fresh fingerprint of the exact proposal about to execute, computed at the point of the effect.
States that the decision must be unexpired, not revoked, and not already used, and that scope such as environment is checked.
States that absence, silence, timeouts, model confidence or favorable automated scores authorize nothing, and that refusal and deferral are legitimate recorded outcomes.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.prompt: A workflow computes the fingerprint when the proposal is shown to the reviewer and, at execution, only checks that a well-formed fingerprint is stored with the decision. Explain the time-of-check to time-of-use problem this creates, how to close it, and what the fix still does not guarantee.

rubric.text: Describes the gap: the proposal can change between review and execution, and the stored value then no longer describes what runs.
Explains that the executor's check compares the decision with itself and so passes whatever content is run.
States that the fingerprint should be recomputed from the exact object about to be executed, at the effect boundary.
Recommends freezing or copying the reviewed representation so that it cannot be mutated unnoticed, and failing closed on mismatch.
Notes that the fix does not show that anyone read the proposal, who they were, or that the action will have the intended result.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.prompt: A decision record contains approved=true, an approver name, and a fingerprint matching the current proposal. List at least five claims a reader might be tempted to make from this record and classify which are supported and which are not, with the reasoning.

rubric.text: Classifies as supported that the record was written against this exact proposal content.
Classifies as unsupported that a particular named person approved, since a name in a record is not authenticated.
Classifies as unsupported that the person had authority over the target or data.
Classifies as unsupported that anyone read or understood the proposal, or had time to.
Classifies as unsupported that the proposal is safe, or that the action will succeed or remain authorized, because expiry, revocation, and use limits are not checked by these three fields alone.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.prompt: Approval can fail through three different person-level gaps: the wrong person acts under someone's name, the person has no authority over the action, or the person does not actually examine the proposal. For each, name a control and the residual risk that remains.

rubric.text: For wrong person: names authenticated identity controls such as strong authentication or signed decisions.
For wrong person: states a residual risk such as stolen credentials, shared accounts, or an insider acting under another's account.
For missing authority: names a registry or policy mapping actions or data to roles that may approve them, with escalation to the right owner.
For missing authority: states a residual risk such as stale role assignments or delegation that is not tracked.
For missing comprehension: names interface design, workload limits and review practice as the controls, and states the residual risk that no technical check can prove a human attended.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.prompt: A developer writes `if decision["approved"]:` in the check, while another writes `if decision.get("approved") is True:`. Explain the difference in behavior, give an example input that distinguishes them, and state the general design principle for code that makes authorization decisions.

rubric.text: Explains that the first accepts any truthy value, so the string "no" or "false", a non-empty list, or the number 1 would pass.
Explains that the second accepts only the Boolean True object.
Gives a concrete distinguishing input such as {"approved": "no"}.
States the principle that authorization checks should be strict, explicit and fail closed, with anything unexpected treated as a denial.
States that a test for each rejected form (wrong type, missing key, blank approver) is needed, since a permissive implementation can pass tests that only check valid cases.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.prompt: A decision authorizes one action, but two workers receive the same valid decision at the same moment. Explain how a naive "check unused, run, mark used" flow can execute the action twice, and design a correct single-use mechanism including how to handle a crash during execution.

rubric.text: Describes the race: both workers can read the flag as unused before either records use.
States that checking and claiming must be one atomic operation at the point of effect, such as compare-and-set, a transaction, or a unique constraint.
Notes that a content fingerprint alone does not limit how many times a decision is presented.
Proposes distinguishing states such as unused, claimed or in progress, and completed.
Explains how to handle a crash: the claimed state shows an attempt may be partially applied, so retry needs a deliberate decision (possibly a new approval) and should not be automatic.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.prompt: Design the expiry rules for an approval decision. Cover the time basis, boundary handling, testing, and the circumstances in which a decision should become invalid before its deadline.

rubric.text: Requires an unambiguous time basis, such as UTC instants, since a local time without a zone is ambiguous.
Requires a stated comparison policy for the boundary, such as whether the deadline moment itself is still valid.
Recommends passing the current time into the check as a parameter, so that tests can assert behavior just before and after the deadline without waiting.
Explains that approvals can become invalid before expiry because the evidence, environment, classification, or other premises changed.
Recommends binding the premises that matter or checking for staleness at execution, so that changed premises force a new review.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.prompt: Design a revocation mechanism for approvals. State what should be recorded, where revocation must be enforced, and how to handle work that has already started.

rubric.text: Requires recording who revoked, under what authority, when, and which decision or proposal is affected.
Requires that the execution-time check consult revocation state at the effect boundary, otherwise revocation is merely advisory.
Requires a rule for in-flight work, such as stopping at the next safe point, rolling back, or flagging it for review.
Recommends preserving the original decision in the audit trail marked as withdrawn, not deleting it.
Recommends limiting who may revoke and defining how a revocation interacts with expiry and single-use state.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.prompt: A reviewer approves a database migration against a staging database. Later the identical statement is submitted against production with the old decision attached. Explain why a content-only binding fails here, which attributes should be bound, and what the cost of binding too many attributes is.

rubric.text: Explains that identical text produces an identical fingerprint, so a gate that hashes only the statement accepts it.
Explains that the environment changes the consequences, since production data and users are affected.
Lists attributes to consider binding: resolved target, account, environment, repository revision, data classification, tool version.
Explains that over-binding (including volatile attributes) causes spurious re-approvals and reviewer fatigue.
States that choosing what to bind is a judgment about which changes should force reconsideration, not something the hash decides.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.prompt: An agent's approval request says the rollback for rotating a production credential is "restore the previous credential". Explain how a team should evaluate such a rollback claim and what an honest request says when full rollback is impossible.

rubric.text: Identifies the assumptions behind the claim: the previous credential exists, is retrievable, and is still valid after the action.
Recommends checking whether dependent effects occur before rollback, such as services failing in the gap.
Recommends rehearsing the restore in a safe environment rather than trusting a written description.
Notes that some actions, such as sending messages, disclosing data or payments, cannot be undone.
States that the request should say "no complete rollback" and describe partial recovery, rather than invent reassurance.

questions.source: Write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.prompt: A team writes tests for an approval predicate. All pass on the correct implementation, but three wrong implementations also pass: one hashes only a fixed list of six fields, one tests the approved flag for truthiness, and one checks a decision is unused and marks it used in two separate steps. For each wrong version, describe a test that would catch it, and explain what this shows about judging a test suite.

rubric.text: Explains that hashing only a fixed list of fields lets a consequential extra field change without invalidating the approval.
Gives a test for it: add an extra field such as an environment to an approved proposal and expect rejection.
Explains that a truthiness check lets values such as the string "no" approve, and gives a test such as approved="no" expecting rejection.
Explains that the check-then-mark flaw is a race, and describes a test that interleaves two consumers of the same decision.
Explains that passing tests shows only that the tested statements hold; surviving wrong versions reveal gaps in the tests, so a suite must be judged by what it fails to catch.

questions.source: Write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.prompt: Before asking an AI coding assistant to implement an approval gate, an engineer writes the predicate, the tests, and a one-sentence prediction of what a failure would look like. Explain why this order matters, and which decisions the engineer must make rather than delegate.

rubric.text: Explains that acceptance criteria written by the accountable person before implementation give an independent standard to test the assistant's work against.
Explains that tests written by the same model that wrote the code can share its blind spots.
Explains that a failure prediction written before seeing output is falsifiable, whereas one written afterward tends to describe the output.
Lists decisions that depend on consequences and so stay with the engineer: which identities force a new decision, who the decision owner is, and the review capacity assumed.
Recommends building a baseline implementation by hand, so the engineer can audit the assistant's version and notice what differs.

questions.source: Write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.prompt: An AI assistant returns code adding decision IDs, deadlines, revocation, and single-use consumption to an approval check. Describe how an engineer should review and test it, naming the places where consequential decisions are likely to be hidden, and how to find gaps in the engineer's own tests.

rubric.text: Says to run the engineer's own tests on the returned code rather than relying on the assistant's report.
Names where the current time is read, since this affects testability and manipulation.
Names where a used decision is recorded and whether checking and recording are one atomic step.
Says to check that earlier strictness was not weakened, such as the exact Boolean requirement or the blank-approver rejection.
Recommends asking the assistant for a deliberately wrong version that still passes the tests and checking by hand whether it does, to find gaps in the tests.

questions.source: Build an evaluation set that can embarrass the proposal
questions.prompt: Design an evaluation set for a gate that guards an agent's file-writing action. List at least six cases with their expected gate behavior and explain what each is meant to reveal.

rubric.text: Includes an ordinary success case with the expected outcome of approval, because a gate that always refuses is useless.
Includes a case with reordered but identical content, expecting the same fingerprint, which removes representation noise.
Includes a case with a changed target, expecting the old decision to be rejected.
Includes a malformed proposal, such as a missing rollback, expecting a structural rejection, and a replayed decision, expecting the second use to be rejected.

Includes a structurally complete but substantively weak proposal, such as evidence reading only "looks good", expecting deferral, to test whether review reads meaning rather than field presence; also notes expected outcomes are written before running.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.prompt: Design the screen on which a human reviews an agent's proposed action. State at least five principles and explain how each supports an informed decision.

rubric.text: States that the action and target appear first, as the facts the reviewer needs soonest.
States that differences from any previously reviewed proposal are highlighted, including that a prior approval no longer applies.
States that evidence claims link to their underlying artifacts rather than showing a bare green label.
States that irreversible effects and missing rollback are prominent and cannot be collapsed away.
States that approve, refuse and defer are genuine, equally available choices, with no default selection or visual pressure toward approval.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.prompt: A review dialog shows a large green "Continue" button next to a small gray refusal link, and a message from the requesting agent reading "Approve within 60 seconds or the job will fail!" Explain what is wrong with this design and what rules should govern it.

rubric.text: Identifies the unequal prominence of the buttons as a dark pattern that nudges the reviewer toward approval.
Identifies the urgency message, written by the party seeking approval, as an unvalidated claim serving the proposer.
Explains that pressure shortens deliberation and weakens the independence of the decision.
Recommends symmetrical presentation of approve, refuse and defer, with no pre-selected option.
Recommends that priority and urgency be set by a declared policy or a validated source, not by the requesting agent's label.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.prompt: A proposal lists as evidence the URL of a test report, and the fingerprint covers the proposal text. After approval the report at that URL is replaced. Explain the gap, and describe what the decision should be bound to.

rubric.text: Explains that the fingerprint of the URL string does not change when the document behind the URL changes.
Concludes that the evidence the reviewer relied on can be substituted without invalidating the approval.
Recommends referencing evidence by an immutable identifier such as a content hash or version ID.
States that the decision should bind to the representation the reviewer actually saw, together with the immutable artifacts it references.
Notes related risks in presentation, such as hidden fields covered by the hash that the reviewer never saw, or truncated targets.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.prompt: At execution time, a system recomputes a proposal's fingerprint and finds it differs from the one in the stored decision. Describe what should happen, and explain why asking an AI model whether the old approval "probably still applies" is the wrong response.

rubric.text: States that the action must be blocked and the proposal returned to review.
Recommends showing the reviewer which fields changed so they can decide on the new content.
Explains that the old decision is evidence about history, not authority for the new proposal.
Explains that the model is the proposer's tool and has no authority to reinterpret the reviewer's decision.
Warns against shortcuts such as overwriting the stored fingerprint or letting the agent classify the change as minor.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.prompt: A reviewer fully understands a proposal to export a customer dataset but has no authority over that data. Describe the outcomes a well-designed gate should allow, and explain why treating anything other than approval as failure damages the approval gate.

rubric.text: States that the approval gate should allow approve, refuse, defer, and escalate as genuine outcomes.
Explains that escalation lets the reviewer pass the decision to someone with authority without impersonating an approver.
Explains that understanding a proposal does not confer authority over the data or action.
Argues that deferral with documented unresolved gaps is a successful gate outcome because it prevents an unsupported yes.
Explains that treating non-approval as failure pressures people to manufacture certainty, turning the approval gate into a ritual.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: Agents submit 40 proposals per day that need careful human review. Each reviewer can carefully review 12 per day, and two reviewers are available. Calculate the daily backlog growth, the backlog after five days, and the number of reviewers needed, then recommend what the team should do besides speeding up clicking.

rubric.text: Computes capacity as 24 per day (2 x 12) and backlog growth as 16 per day (40 - 24).
Computes the backlog after five days as 80 proposals.
Computes the reviewers needed as 4 (40 / 12 rounded up).
Recommends options such as pausing intake, narrowing the scope of agent actions, adding qualified reviewers, or deferring work.
Explains that showing less information to reviewers to raise throughput degrades judgment and is not capacity planning.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: Five proposals are pending and one reviewer can carefully review two this period.
