A is a reversible local formatting change, B sends material to an external recipient, C changes a production target, D duplicates B's effect, and E depends on C being approved. Propose a queue policy and justify it.

rubric.text: Prioritizes B and C because their effects are external or high-impact.
Detects D as a likely duplicate of B and holds it rather than spending review on it.
Keeps E blocked on the decision about C.
Lets A wait, expire, or proceed only under a separately authorized low-risk policy.
States that the policy must be set by accountable people before agents label their own work, and that proposer-supplied urgency labels must not set priority unvalidated.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: A team finds that reviewers approve 99.6% of proposals in a median of 8 seconds, and a dashboard ranks reviewers by throughput. Diagnose what may be wrong, and propose changes to the process and measurements.

rubric.text: Identifies habituation or rubber-stamping as a possible explanation for the very high approval rate and short review time.
Notes that a high approval rate alone does not show that proposals are good or that decisions were informed.
Recommends checking whether reviewers have real options, sufficient evidence, and support for saying no.
Recommends tracking refusal, deferral and later-reversed approvals as measures of review quality.
Explains that ranking reviewers by throughput rewards speed over care and should be replaced by measures of decision quality.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: Reviewers keep receiving nearly identical low-consequence proposals, such as formatting changes to documentation in a sandbox repository. Discuss whether and how a standing policy could replace individual approvals for this class.

rubric.text: Says that it is a governance decision owned by accountable people, not a shortcut the agent can take.
Requires the class to be defined precisely so that membership is unambiguous.
Requires testing the exclusions: cases just outside the class must still be routed to a reviewer.
Requires monitoring of outcomes and a way to revoke the policy.
States that everything outside the class remains gated and that the policy must not drift to adjacent classes without review.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: A pipeline lets an action proceed if no reviewer responds within 30 minutes, if the agent reports confidence above 0.95, or if an automated evaluation score is at least 90%. Argue why none of these constitutes authorization and describe what legitimate automation of approvals looks like.

rubric.text: Argues that a timeout is the absence of a decision, not consent.
Argues that a model's self-reported confidence is neither a calibrated measure nor a decision by someone with authority.
Argues that an evaluation score is evidence about tested cases and not permission.
Notes that destructive or irreversible actions make these shortcuts especially risky.
Describes legitimate automation as a narrowly defined standing policy set in advance by accountable people, with monitoring and revocation.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: A team adopts agents that generate 10 times as many proposals per day (200 instead of 20), while reviewers can still carefully review 20 per day. Calculate what share can be carefully reviewed and explain the consequences and design responses.

rubric.text: Computes that 20 of 200 is 10% that can be carefully reviewed.
Explains that generation scales with compute while careful verification does not scale with it.
Explains that proposals that proceed unreviewed are effectively unverified, so more output means less oversight per item.
Rejects the idea that skimming or using the same model to review restores independent judgment.
Recommends treating review capacity as a design constraint: measure or declare it, limit intake or scope to match, and report honestly when safe throughput is below production rate.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: A marketing manager is asked to approve an agent's proposed database migration. The proposal is fluent and its claims sound reasonable, but it contains a subtle locking problem that would cause an outage. Explain why the review can fail even though the reviewer is diligent, and what the organization should do about it.

rubric.text: Explains that judging whether a claim is credible relies on the reviewer's own domain knowledge, so errors outside it are not noticed.
Notes that fluent, confident text is not evidence of correctness, and an agent's own explanation of safety is another claim the reviewer cannot verify.
Recommends routing each proposal to a reviewer able to audit it, and sending proposals outside the reviewer's field to a specialist.
Recommends support such as deterministic checks, tests, or an expert's analysis as evidence the non-expert can rely on.
Recommends keeping reviewer workload low enough for judgment and tracking which reviewer each proposal went to and why.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.prompt: Describe a feedback loop that uses what happens after approvals to improve a gate. Include what is compared, what is inspected, and how findings change the evaluation process.

rubric.text: Compares the effects predicted in proposals with the outcomes actually observed.
Inspects approvals that were later reversed and asks what evidence or support the reviewer lacked.
Tracks refusals and deferrals as well as approvals, to see whether reviewers have real options.
Updates the next evaluation set after any unexpected outcome, harmless or not, before further approvals are requested.
Avoids scoring reviewers on throughput, which would train the approval gate toward ceremony.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.prompt: An engineer's sign-off for a newly built approval gate reads in full: "Reviewed by the team. All tests passed. The approval gate is safe for production. Approved." Critique this sign-off and explain what a useful one would contain.

rubric.text: Notes that it does not say which checks were run, against which criteria, or what the results were.
Notes that it does not say what was not tested or which failure modes were not reached, which is what makes a sign-off honest.
Notes that "the team" is not a person or role who can be asked and who answers if the approval gate was cleared wrongly.
Notes that "safe for production" overclaims, and that verbs should match the strength of the evidence (passed a stated test versus believed safe).
Describes a better form: what was tested and how, what was not tested, who cleared which gate, calibrated verbs, and an explicit statement of what is not being claimed.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.prompt: An engineer asks an AI assistant, without providing any test logs or notes, to write the sign-off statement for her validation work. It returns a fluent paragraph naming a reviewer and asserting that a full review took place. Explain why this paragraph is empty and how a truthful sign-off should be produced.

rubric.text: Explains that a language model has no knowledge of what was tested or skipped unless it is given the record.
Explains that the paragraph has the shape of a sign-off without substance, and shape is easy to produce.
Notes that a reviewer's name or confident wording in generated text is not evidence that any review took place.
States that the engineer should write the statement from her own record of tests run, results, and gaps, using the assistant at most for wording.
States that a signer must be able to support every claim and should withhold the signature if the record does not.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.prompt: A release process requires the test lead's signature, and in two years the lead has never declined to sign. Explain what this suggests, why the signer's right to withhold matters, and how the process could be changed so that a signature carries information.

rubric.text: Explains that if signing is the only permitted outcome, the process is a rubber stamp that hides missing review behind a name.
Explains that a signature only carries information if refusing or deferring is a real possibility.
Recommends making withholding and deferral legitimate, recorded outcomes, not process failures.
Recommends giving the signer authority, time, and an escalation path, so declining does not cost them.
Recommends tracking how often sign-offs are withheld or conditioned and what happened afterward.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.prompt: The engineer who built an evaluation gate must write its sign-off, and finds she wants to write "no known issues." Explain the bias at work and describe practices that counter it.

rubric.text: Identifies ownership bias: builders tend to overrate and under-examine their own work.
Recommends requiring a minimum number of entries (for example, three) in a "not tested" section.
Recommends noting for each untested item whether it was skipped as out of scope or because time ran out.
Recommends asking whether any untested condition is where harm would be most likely.
Recommends independent review of the sign-off, and notes that being unable to list gaps suggests insufficient scrutiny rather than a perfect system.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.prompt: A company adopts named sign-offs for high-risk automated actions. Discuss what this regime provides, what it costs, and why accountability should not rest only on the person who signed or clicked.

rubric.text: States that it provides answerability: after a failure one can find who signed, read what they claimed and what they said they did not warrant.
States that it costs speed, because documenting limits takes effort, and removes deniability for the signer.
Notes that under schedule pressure, questions about what was not tested will be felt as friction, and the process may route around them.
Argues that governance should name organizational owners and escalation paths, not push every consequence onto the individual who clicked.
Notes that a signature strengthens identity evidence but does not prove comprehension or competence.

questions.source: Where the approval step sits in the build so far
questions.prompt: Describe the sequence of steps that takes an agent's proposed action from construction to observed outcome in a sound approval workflow, and explain what happens when the proposal is changed after approval.

rubric.text: Describes constructing the proposal from the plan and current state, then validating required fields and policy boundaries.
Describes running scoped evaluations and recording what they do not cover.
Describes freezing the exact proposal and computing its fingerprint before presenting evidence and consequences to an authorized reviewer.
Describes recording approve, refuse or defer against that fingerprint, and rechecking fingerprint, expiry, revocation and use limits at execution.
Explains that a changed proposal returns to evaluation and review, and that the actual outcome is observed and stored as a separate record afterward.

questions.source: Where the approval step sits in the build so far
questions.prompt: An approved action runs, its fingerprint check passes, and a later check shows the file contains the wrong content. Explain why the fingerprint, the effect evidence, and the post-action check should be kept as separate linked records, and what each shows.

rubric.text: States that approval permits a bounded attempt and does not guarantee the intended result.
States that the fingerprint shows the executed proposal was the approved one.
States that effect evidence, such as a trace, shows what the executor actually did.
States that the post-action check shows the resulting state of the world.
Explains that merging them hides which link failed, and that keeping them separate lets a team locate whether the proposal, the execution, or the outcome was wrong.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.prompt: A developer configures an agent to run any command matching the pattern "npm run *" without asking. One repository defines a script named "cleanup" that deletes a user's project directory. Explain what this reveals about approval by pattern, and propose a safer permission policy.

rubric.text: Explains that the pattern approves a form of command, not the effects of what the script does, which can be arbitrary.
Notes that the script's content is controlled by the repository, which may be untrusted or changed later.
Proposes narrower allow rules, such as specific named scripts, and explicit deny rules for destructive commands.
Proposes isolation controls such as a sandbox, least-privilege credentials, or running in a disposable environment.
States that any pre-approval is a standing authorization that should be scoped, reviewed periodically, and revocable.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.prompt: Describe a sound division of labor between an AI assistant and a human in an approval gate. Name tasks for each and explain why the human tasks cannot be delegated.

rubric.text: Assigns the assistant drafting the structured proposal, flagging fields it could not fill, and showing changes from the last proposal.
Assigns the assistant running checkers, grouping traces, and flagging missing rollback or evidence.
Assigns the human choosing the cases that can embarrass the proposal, recording exclusions, and deciding which changes force a new decision.
Assigns the human approving, refusing, deferring or escalating within their authority.
Explains that authority and accountability attach to a person, that attention is finite, and that the assistant should stop at the authorization boundary and keep the action queued.

questions.source: Ship It: a gate design that survives a skeptical reader
questions.prompt: A student's prototype gate fingerprints proposals and verifies that the decision has an approved flag and a nonblank approver string. List at least five things that must be added or established before relying on it in production, and state what the student can and cannot honestly claim about it.

rubric.text: Lists authenticated identity for approvers, since a name string can be typed by anyone.
Lists an authority registry saying who may approve which actions.
Lists expiry, revocation and atomic single-use consumption.
Lists audit logging with access control and retention, queue and capacity behavior, and an incident-response path.
States the honest claims: content binding under a simulated approver; and not that any person reviewed, was authorized, or that the proposal is safe.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: A manager says: "We added an approval step to our agent pipeline, so human oversight is guaranteed." Respond by describing at least five ways such a step can exist and still fail to provide oversight.

rubric.text: Notes that the approval may be bound to something other than the executed content, so drift or substitution can occur.
Notes that the reviewer may lack the information, such as target, effects or rollback, needed to decide.
Notes that the reviewer may lack authority or the domain expertise to detect problems.
Notes that review capacity may be exceeded so that decisions become reflexive clicks or are skipped by timeouts.
Notes that interface pressure, a record with no genuine refusal option, or an unverified identity can turn the step into a ritual.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint

rubric.text: Identifies that only six fields are hashed, so changes to any other field of the proposal do not invalidate the approval; fix by hashing the entire proposal (or an explicit full set).
Identifies that json.dumps is called without sorted keys or fixed separators, so equivalent proposals can hash differently; fix with canonical serialization.
Identifies that the approved and approver checks use truthiness, so "no" or a whitespace-only name passes; fix with approved is True and a stripped, nonblank (ideally authenticated) approver.
Identifies that the used set is checked and then updated in separate steps in process memory, so concurrent workers can both pass; fix with an atomic claim in a shared store.
Identifies missing expiry, revocation and clock handling, and fragile error handling such as KeyError on missing keys; fix by adding these checks and returning a denial on any malformed input.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: A team must choose how to check three things in its gate: that a proposal is valid JSON with six required fields, that a rollback plan is plausible and specific, and that releasing a customer dataset is acceptable. Choose a type of grader (deterministic code, model-based, or human) for each and justify the choices.

rubric.text: Chooses deterministic code for the JSON and field check, because it is mechanical, cheap and reliable.
Chooses a model-based grader, calibrated against human-labeled examples, for judging plausibility and specificity of free-text rollback plans, or a human, with the reasoning.
Notes that model-based grading has failure modes such as fluent but wrong text and shared biases, so its scores are evidence rather than decisions.
Chooses a human with authority for the dataset release, because it is a judgment about consequence and permission.
Recommends combining graders, keeping deterministic checks where possible and human review proportional to stakes.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.prompt: An approval workflow reports four things: the share of tasks the agent completed, whether actions complied with policy, how much effort reviewers spent, and whether an authorized person approved each consequential action. Explain why these are separate questions and why a high value on one does not imply the others.

rubric.text: States that task success measures whether the work was done, and an agent can complete tasks by violating policy.
States that policy compliance is checked against stated rules and says nothing about whether a responsible person permitted an exception.
States that reviewer burden can fall because information was hidden or reviewers click reflexively, not because decisions were well informed.
States that authorization concerns a person with authority deciding, which no automated score can supply.
Recommends reporting the four separately, with errors and deferrals included, so that tradeoffs between them are visible.

questions.source: Ship It: a gate design that survives a skeptical reader
questions.prompt: Build a threat model for an approval gate covering these threats: mutation of the proposal after it is shown, target aliasing, replay of a decision, stolen reviewer identity, reviewer overload, a misleading rollback claim, and revoked approval. For at least five of them, name a control, say whether it is code or a human practice, and state a residual risk.

rubric.text: For mutation after display: recompute the fingerprint at the effect boundary (code); residual risk is that the displayed representation may differ from the hashed one.
For target aliasing: bind resolved identifiers and show canonical paths (code); residual risk is changes to what an identifier points to.
For replay: use decision IDs with atomic single-use consumption and expiry (code); residual risk is crash and retry ambiguity.
For stolen identity and reviewer overload: authenticated, signed decisions (code) and workload limits with escalation (people); residual risk is stolen credentials, habituation, and capacity.

For misleading rollback and revoked approval: test the rollback and state partial recovery honestly (people), and check revocation at execution (code); residual risk is unforeseen dependent effects and in-flight work.

questions.source: Opening: a complete register is not a responsible team
questions.prompt: A team's AI-use register has every required field filled. The owner field reads "project team", the incident contact reads "project owner" and the evaluation field reads "citation audit". A script that checks only that fields are non-empty reports the record as ready for human review. Explain how a register can be complete and the workflow still have no one responsible, and say what question a reviewer should ask instead of "is the register complete?"

rubric.text: A record can be structurally complete yet operationally hollow: presence of text in a field is not the same as a decision having been made.
Group or role labels such as "project team" do not identify a person who has accepted responsibility, and a vague evaluation line does not say what was tested.
A completeness script checks structure only, so it can truthfully report a green status while no one is accountable, no affected person was consulted and no threshold triggers any response.
The status "ready for review" is not approval, consent, compliance or an ethical judgment.
The better question is what "complete" stands in for: what has been decided, who decided it, and who will answer when the system causes harm.

questions.source: Opening: what Claude can and cannot do in a governance register
questions.prompt: A teammate says: "An LLM can fill the whole governance register in seconds, so the governance work is done." Respond. Say what a language model can and cannot contribute, and describe how responsibilities divide between the model and the humans in the team.

rubric.text: The model can draft fluent, plausible proposals quickly, such as an owner, a threshold, a retention period and a risk paragraph.
It cannot make anyone the owner it names: accountability exists only when a person accepts it.
It has no first-hand contact with the people affected and is not answerable for the workflow after the conversation ends.
Humans decide and record the key choices (owners, thresholds, retention, consultation, recourse) before the form is filled, and check that a complete-looking register is not weak.
Relationships, consent, recourse and the decision to ship, narrow or stop remain with people, who also sign or withhold the final sign-off.

questions.source: Teardown of the validator: what a status means
questions.prompt: A validator reports one of three statuses for a governance record: "incomplete", "review-required" and "ready-for-human-review". Write precise one-sentence descriptions of what "ready-for-human-review" and "review-required" each claim, and explain what stronger claims would need as evidence.

rubric.text: "Ready for human review" means the record cleared the validator's structural checks and nothing was flagged; it describes the record's shape.
"Review required" means the validator found a condition it cannot resolve (for example an unknown data class) and is routing the decision to a person.
Neither status states that a human has reviewed, approved or accepted anything.
Claims of approval would need an identifiable authorized person who approved a specific proposal on a specific date.
Claims of consent or legal compliance would need evidence from the affected individuals or from legal review respectively, which a script cannot supply.

questions.source: Who decided? Five choices that exist before the form does
questions.prompt: Five decisions underlie any governance record for an AI workflow: owner, threshold, retention, consultation and recourse. Define each in one sentence as an assignment of authority or responsibility, and explain why a team should make these decisions before it fills in a governance form.

rubric.text: Owner: the person who accepts responsibility for the workflow as an ongoing system and has authority to stop it.
Threshold: the observable signal that triggers a response, together with what the response is.
Retention: which copies of data exist, for how long, and how deletion is performed and checked.
Consultation: who was asked, what their answers could have changed, and what remains pending; recourse: how an affected person reaches a human who can change the outcome.
Each is an assignment of authority that exists only when someone accepts it; filling the form first yields the shape of a decision and anchors reviewers to a draft instead of a decision.

questions.source: Who decided? Five choices that exist before the form does
questions.prompt: A team cannot find anyone willing to accept ownership of a planned LLM workflow that will send e-mails to customers. Describe how the team should record this gap, what constraints they should place on the workflow until the gap is closed, and why they should not simply put a placeholder name in the owner field.

rubric.text: The gap should be recorded explicitly as unresolved, not filled with a plausible name.
A placeholder name creates the appearance of accountability without anyone having accepted it.
Until someone accepts ownership, the workflow should be constrained, for example to private drafts, synthetic data, or no external writes.
The constraints should be tied to a condition for lifting them, such as a named person accepting the role with authority to pause.
Assigning every role to one person or to the AI agent merely to complete the form does not solve the gap, because the owner must be someone who can accept and exercise responsibility.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.prompt: Before asking an LLM assistant to implement a validator for a governance record, a developer writes a specification (what must pass, what must raise errors, what must be flagged) and a set of tests. Explain what the developer gains by doing this first and what the developer should do with the assistant's implementation afterward.

rubric.text: Writing the contract first forces decisions about edge cases (such as zero retention and wrong input types) to be made by the person, not inherited from the model.
Tests written before seeing the implementation capture the person's intent independently of the code.
Running the tests on the assistant's implementation, personally, shows whether it satisfies the specification; failures can expose gaps in the specification itself.
The developer can ask for a deliberately wrong implementation that still passes the tests; if one exists, the test suite is too weak.
Building a baseline first gives the developer a concrete reference to name differences in behavior between versions, which is what auditing requires.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.prompt: A Python function validates a retention-day count with `isinstance(days, int) and days >= 0`. Explain what happens for the inputs True, 0, 30.0 and -1, why exact type checking such as `type(days) is int` changes one of these results, and what a test suite needs to include to detect the isinstance version.

rubric.text: True is accepted by the isinstance version because bool is a subclass of int in Python, so True behaves as 1.
0 is accepted, which is correct if zero retention is a legitimate design intent.
30.0 is rejected because a float is not an int instance, and -1 is rejected by the range test.
`type(days) is int` rejects True because type(True) is bool, not int.
The suite needs a test that expects True to be rejected, and ideally the zero and negative boundary cases, so that an isinstance implementation fails.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.prompt: A validator treats a field as missing if `not record.get(field)` is true. Describe two kinds of wrong behavior this causes for a record with `retention_days: 0` and for a record with `owner: "   "` (spaces only), and propose a better missing-field test and how to treat blank text.

rubric.text: Zero is falsy, so a deliberate zero-day retention value is wrongly reported as missing.
A whitespace-only string is truthy and so is accepted as present although it names no one.
The better presence test distinguishes absence (key not present or value is None) from other values, so zero is retained as a legitimate value.
For text fields, normalize with strip() and then reject empty strings.
These are narrow structural fixes; they still cannot tell whether a non-empty owner is a real accountable person.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.prompt: A validator for data labels uses an allowlist (public, synthetic, internal) and sends anything else to human review. Explain why an allowlist routing unknown values to review is a conservative design, what costs it imposes, and what it cannot establish about the data.

rubric.text: When the machine cannot classify a label, sending the decision to a person is the safe default.
An allowlist catches categories nobody listed in advance, unlike a denylist.
Costs include reviewer workload and false alarms, such as a case-sensitive comparison sending "Public" to review.
The check cannot determine whether an unknown label is actually sensitive, nor whether an allowed label such as "internal" is appropriate for the specific use.
It also does not verify that the data was assigned its label correctly in the first place.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.prompt: Explain why a governance validator should refuse only what it can refuse exactly, and what kinds of judgment it should leave to people. Give two examples of checks that belong in code and two judgments that belong to humans.

rubric.text: Code is reliable on exact, mechanical conditions, such as required fields present, correct types and ranges, and membership in a list.
Judgments about adequacy, such as whether an owner line names an accountable person or an evaluation line is a real test, depend on context that string checks cannot encode.
A deny-list of "bad phrases" would be evaded by rewording, so it gives false assurance.
Examples in code: type and range checks on retention; flagging unknown data classes. Examples for humans: whether an owner has accepted the role; whether an evaluation tests the relevant harm.
A validator that claims only what it checks is more honest than one that implies quality assessment.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.prompt: A validator adds the issue "external action approval" whenever a record's `external_write` value is truthy. Describe what this check does and does not accomplish, and name two Python pitfalls in relying on truthiness for such a flag.

rubric.text: It marks that an external action is involved and routes the record to an approval control.
It does not verify that approval was obtained, who approved, or what the external target is.
Non-empty strings such as "no" and "false" are truthy, so a mistyped flag can trigger or fail to trigger the check.
Values like 0, None or an empty string are falsy and will silently skip the check, so required Boolean type enforcement is needed.
The flag is a routing signal; a separate control must bind approval to the exact proposed action.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.prompt: Construct a record that passes a structural validator (all fields present and well formed) but is weak as governance, and for each of three vague lines write the question a named person would need to answer and the act that would answer it.

rubric.text: The example includes vague entries such as owner "everyone", evaluation "looks fine" and incident contact "team".
Owner: "Who personally accepts responsibility and can pause the workflow?" answered by a named person confirming acceptance.
Evaluation: "What outcomes were tested, by whom, on what data, and what happens on failure?" answered by a documented test with criteria and sampling.
Incident contact: "Can an affected person reach a human who can act?" answered by sending a labeled test report and observing acknowledgment within the stated time.
The structural validator is not defective for passing such a record; its contract is narrow, which is why human review must interrogate meaning.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.prompt: A reviewer is writing up what a governance validation run and a test of an incident-reporting route established. Explain how to word each claim so it is no stronger than the evidence behind it. Illustrate with claims about the incident route at three or more levels of evidence, from weakest to strongest, naming the evidence each level needs.

rubric.text: The principle: the wording of a claim should match what was actually done, so a script that checked structure "reported" presence and did not "confirm" anyone's acceptance.
Weakest level: a name or role appears in a document, which supports only "is listed".
Next level: the named person has said they accept the role, which supports "has agreed".
Stronger level: the route was run and observed to work, for example a clearly labeled test report was acknowledged within the stated time.
Strongest level: the reviewer inspected the system or store directly, and claims about systems that were not inspected must stay at the weaker levels.

questions.source: A register makes questions inspectable
questions.prompt: A summarizer was approved for public course notes. Months later it is pointed at student-submitted essays. Explain how a well-written purpose statement helps detect this change, why the change needs fresh review even if the model and prompt are unchanged, and what a purpose line like "use AI" fails to do.

rubric.text: A precise purpose bounds what the system is for, so a new use can be recognized as out of scope.
Student essays involve different people, different data classes and different consequences, so risk changes even with identical model and prompt.
The change should trigger review of data classes, consent, retention, evaluation and who is affected.
"Use AI" excludes nothing, so no later use can be flagged as beyond scope.
Scope creep tends to go unnoticed unless the purpose is stated precisely and reviewed when use changes.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.prompt: Rewrite the vague promise "monitor quality and intervene if needed" as an operational control for an LLM tool that publishes summaries. Your rewrite should specify the signal, threshold, owner, response, scope and recovery condition, and you should explain what makes a threshold testable by a stranger.

rubric.text: Signal: an observable measure, such as published summaries containing a claim without a supporting source.
Threshold and owner: a numeric or event trigger (for example any single such claim) and a named person responsible for acting.
Response and scope: publication pauses, affected drafts are examined, and the scope of what pauses is defined.
Recovery condition: work resumes only after correction and a repeated check passes.
A stranger can tell from the record whether it fired because the signal, trigger and response are observable and unambiguous.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.prompt: An LLM service processed 20,000 requests last month and an automated check passed 99.5% of them. A manual review of the failures found that 2 of them exposed customers' personal data. Calculate how many failures there were, explain why the pass rate alone is an inadequate governance signal, and propose a better trigger design.

rubric.text: 0.5% of 20,000 is 100 failures.
The aggregate rate weights all failures equally, so rare severe events are hidden inside the average.
Two disclosures among 100 failures are a severity category the pass rate does not display.
Severe harms warrant a stop-on-first-occurrence trigger and separate monitoring by harm category.
Less severe failures can use a trend or rate threshold, and the trigger design should specify who can pause and what the response is.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.prompt: An organization names an incident owner for an AI pipeline but rewards on-time delivery and penalizes delays. Explain why the owner cannot effectively govern in that environment and what must change for the role to work.

rubric.text: Authority to pause must be explicit; a nominal owner who has to ask permission cannot respond quickly.
If delay is penalized, people will avoid using pause authority, so it exists only on paper.
The cost of pausing should be assigned in advance to the organization, not to the individual who triggers it.
Escalation must be defined for cases when the owner is unavailable, implicated or lacks expertise.
Incentives and metrics should be aligned so that exercising the control is not punished, and the team should test that the pause actually works.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.prompt: The incident contact for an AI service is unreachable during a possible data exposure and nobody acknowledges an alert within the declared window. Describe what a well-designed response structure does, what it means if no backup exists, and why the AI system should not name itself as the responsible party.

rubric.text: A named backup with delegated pause authority is alerted after the acknowledgment window, pauses the service and records why.
If there is no backup, the exercise has found an unresolved dependency that people must fix.
The AI system cannot accept accountability, so naming itself responsible leaves no accountable person.
The system may safely stop its own work as a default, while responsibility remains with an authorized person or organization.
The rehearsal result should be fed back into the governance record as a change (add a backup, shorten the window) instead of left as an observation.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.prompt: An AI system publishes a summary stating a wrong assignment deadline. Its evaluation was an audit confirming that each cited source identifier exists. Explain why the audit failed to protect against this harm and describe three changes that would address it.

rubric.text: The audit checked that a citation exists, not that the cited material supports the claim.
The harm mechanism is reliance on a false date, and the audit did not address that mechanism.
Change one: add a check for support of consequential claims, by a person or an entailment-style method.
Change two: pause publication and correct existing copies, with a record of copies that cannot be reached.
Change three: assign a named owner with pause authority and define the acknowledgment, triage and escalation steps for the reporting route.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.prompt: A team writes a governance plan before building an AI feature. After an incident they discover one of the plan's decisions was wrong. Explain why designing governance before implementation does not mean it is frozen, and describe how the record should show what changed.

rubric.text: Design before implementation sets the starting decisions; evidence from operation can show that one was inadequate.
An incident can reopen an earlier choice, such as an evaluation that did not test the harm that occurred.
The record should state what the incident revealed, which earlier decision it reopened, and what changed.
Changes should name who made them and when, so the revised decision has an owner.
A record that is never revised after an incident suggests that the feedback loop from operation to design is not working.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.prompt: A register states "retention: 30 days" for user prompts sent to an LLM application. List the copies of the data that may exist beyond the primary store, explain why the stated number does not show that deletion follows it, and describe how to verify deletion for the copies the team controls.

rubric.text: Copies include application logs, caches, backups, exported reports, repository or ticket history, incident records, and the model provider's handling under its own terms.
The number states a policy for one store; other copies follow their own lifecycles and may outlast it.
Define for each class when the retention clock starts, who deletes, and how deletion is checked.
Test by inserting a labeled record, running the lifecycle, and inspecting the stores the team controls.
State what remains unverified, such as the provider and backups, instead of claiming erasure everywhere.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.prompt: A design document sets retention to zero days for a workflow that handles customer messages. Explain what zero could mean, what it does not guarantee, and why a validator should not report zero as a missing value.

rubric.text: Zero could mean delete immediately after the task, do not persist application data, or retain only de-identified evidence.
Data still exists transiently in memory and in any third-party processing, subject to the provider's terms.
A stated value is a design intent and does not show that no copies exist.
A validator that treats falsy values as missing wrongly reports zero as absent; it should test for absence directly.
The design document should define what zero means so that reviewers can check it.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.prompt: A team deletes a customer's row from its application database after a deletion request. The same customer's data also fed a vector index, a weekly summary and a log of hashed e-mail addresses. Explain why the deletion may be incomplete and how the team should handle derived data.

rubric.text: Derived artifacts such as embeddings and summaries can retain or reveal source information.
Hashes of guessable identifiers can be matched against a small known set, so they can still identify the person.
The team needs lineage records showing which artifacts derive from which sources.
Deletion should be tested end to end with labeled data, and each store marked verified or unverified.
Copies the team cannot alter, such as immutable backups, should be listed and disclosed as a limitation.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.prompt: Compare three approaches to logging an AI agent's actions: keep everything forever, keep nothing, and keep a minimal audit record. Describe the trade-offs and propose what the minimal record should contain.

rubric.text: Keeping everything improves investigation and replay but increases privacy exposure and breach impact.
Keeping nothing minimizes retained risk but makes incident investigation and accountability difficult.
A minimal audit record can include operation identity, the policy decision taken, references to evidence stored elsewhere, an error category and responsible roles.
Sensitive payloads should be kept only when justified and should be protected and separated.
The audit record itself needs a retention decision and access controls.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.prompt: A team claims two LLM agents are equally risky because both score 92% on the same 500-item evaluation. Agent A reads public notes, drafts locally and needs a person to publish. Agent B reads internal HR records, publishes externally and keeps year-long traces. Argue which needs stronger governance, calculating each agent's error count, and say why accuracy does not settle the question.

rubric.text: Each agent made 40 errors, since 8% of 500 is 40.
Agent B has a broader action surface, since it writes externally, and a longer exposure window.
B handles more sensitive context, so each error can do more damage.
Accuracy describes selected outputs under selected trials; it does not describe the consequences, reversibility or who is affected.
Architecture choices such as data minimization, human publication and short retention shape harm before any score is computed, so ethics should not be added after model selection.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.prompt: Two summarizers make the same number of deadline errors on the same test set. One states unsupported deadlines. The other omits the deadline when sources conflict. Explain who bears each kind of error, why identical accuracy does not tell which to prefer, and who should make the choice.

rubric.text: Users who plan around a wrong date bear the unsupported-deadline error.
Users who must ask for clarification, and those who handle their questions, bear the omission.
The accuracy figure hides the type of error and so cannot choose between them.
Preferring one error is a value judgment about whose costs count.
The choice should belong to the party accountable for the policy the tool serves, made and recorded deliberately.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.prompt: A classifier is applied to two groups with base rates of 50% and 20%. For both groups the true positive rate is 0.8 and the false positive rate is 0.2. Calculate the positive predictive value for each group, explain what this shows about fairness criteria, and say what follows for decision-making.

rubric.text: For the first group, 40 true positives and 10 false positives per 100 people give precision 0.80.
For the second group, 16 true positives and 16 false positives per 100 give precision 0.50.
Equal error rates across groups coexist with unequal precision when base rates differ.
Several reasonable fairness criteria cannot all hold together at once unless prediction is perfect or base rates match.
Selecting a criterion is a values decision with an owner, who must record whose errors count and what evidence would change the choice.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.prompt: A hiring tool ranks applicants. The team reports 90% overall agreement with past hiring decisions, measured on a set built from people who were hired. Identify who bears false positives and false negatives, critique the evaluation set, and list questions about distribution of burden the team should ask.

rubric.text: Applicants wrongly rejected bear false negatives; recruiters and others bear the cost of reviewing false positives.
An evaluation set built only from hired people hides how the model treats those never hired.
Overall agreement says nothing about how errors fall across subgroups.
Questions include who benefits, who corrects errors, who is absent from development examples, who can opt out, and who can reach a human.
Whether a rejected applicant can reach a human with power to change the outcome is a governance property the accuracy figure does not capture.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a generic risk statement and a concrete harm description in an AI risk register. Write an example of each for an AI summarizer of course notes and say what the concrete one lets a team do.

rubric.text: A generic statement such as "there may be bias or privacy concerns" is not tied to a person, mechanism or consequence and can fit any system.
A concrete statement names who is affected, how the harm arises and what the consequence is.
Example: a student relies on an AI summary giving a wrong deadline and misses the real one.
It lets the team design a test, set a threshold, assign an owner and choose a mitigation that targets that mechanism.
It also enables questions about who pays for the error and who could have prevented it.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: A team plans to consult people affected by a new AI workflow. Describe how to design consultation so it is real, including who to include, what can change as a result, how to ask questions, and what to promise.

rubric.text: Identify directly affected people, maintainers of the surrounding work, domain experts and groups usually missing from design decisions; one convenient person cannot stand in for all.
Consultation counts only if the answers could change purpose, boundaries, retention or the decision to automate.
Participation should be voluntary where appropriate, with explanation of what is recorded, how it is used and whether declining has consequences.
Questions should invite disagreement: what would be unacceptable, what must never enter the workflow, what would make you withdraw support.
Do not promise every request will be adopted; explain how decisions and conflicts will be recorded.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: A team uses an LLM to role-play affected stakeholders, and the model answers agreeably. Explain what this can and cannot show, and how the team's records should treat simulated responses.

rubric.text: Role-play can reveal unclear explanations and missing questions.
It cannot show what real people think; the model produces plausible text, not testimony.
Invented agreement is not consent, which only an informed person can give.
Simulated responses should be labeled as simulation in the record.
The record should state which real consultation remains pending and which actions are prohibited until it occurs.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: After a stakeholder interview, a team uses an LLM to summarize what participants said. Later one participant withdraws permission for their contribution. Describe how the team should keep actual statements distinct from summaries, and what the withdrawal requires of the team's data practices.

rubric.text: Keep the participant's actual words or notes separate from AI-generated summaries.
Return a summary to the participant for confirmation where appropriate.
Record concrete design changes and unresolved concerns that came from the conversation.
To honor a withdrawal, the team must know which artifacts derive from the participant's contribution, such as quotes, embeddings and evaluation examples.
Where removal is impossible, for example from an immutable backup, the limitation should be disclosed to the participant.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: An LLM drafts a plain-language explanation of an AI workflow for affected people. Describe what the explanation should include, why a person must check it against the real system before sharing, and what a careful check looks for.

rubric.text: It should cover what the workflow receives, what it produces, where a person decides, what is retained and how to report a problem.
Fluent simplification can omit exactly the external write or retention detail that matters to the reader.
The checker compares each claim in the draft with the actual system configuration.
The check looks for omitted data flows, overstated human review and understated retention.
Being readable is not evidence of accuracy, so the checker should be someone who knows the system.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: Describe the components of a recourse path for people affected by an AI-assisted decision, and explain why a contact e-mail address is not enough.

rubric.text: A discoverable channel with guidance on what information helps without forcing the person to reveal more private data.
An acknowledgment rule, a triage owner and an urgent-stop trigger.
Investigation access to the contested output, inputs and policy, and power to correct the outcome.
Escalation when the first contact cannot resolve the issue, including a second route when the original owner is conflicted.
An email address alone has no staffing, authority, timing or escalation behind it, so it can be an inbox nobody owns.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: Explain why different harms from an AI error need different remedies, using three examples, and state the five questions a team can ask to test whether a recourse route works.

rubric.text: Correcting a displayed summary does not repair a decision already made from it.
Removing personal data from an active store does not recall a public copy.
Explaining a model's reasoning does not restore an opportunity that was denied.
Test questions: can the person challenge the result, obtain an appropriate explanation, reach a human who can correct the record, see downstream copies updated, and appeal beyond the original owner?
The affected person should be asked what meaningful correction would look like, within institutional limits.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: Describe how a team should make contesting an AI-assisted decision practical: what it must preserve, who reviews, what the reviewer can do, how it handles conflicts of interest, and how it closes the loop with engineering.

rubric.text: Preserve the contested output, input provenance where lawful, the applicable policy and the human decision record.
Reviewers must have the power to change the result.
Provide a second route when the original owner is conflicted.
State response times only when the team can meet them.
If the same class of report keeps recurring while only the reply changes, the process is absorbing complaints; fix the system.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.prompt: A student reports that a published AI summary contradicts the official schedule. Investigation shows the student compared it with an outdated schedule and the published date is correct. Explain how a well-designed contest route should respond and what this shows about contestability.

rubric.text: Acknowledge and investigate the report rather than dismiss it.
Explain the evidence supporting the published date to the reporter.
Preserve the challenge in the record.
Check whether the wording of the summary created reasonable ambiguity.
Contestability means a person can trigger genuine reconsideration; it does not mean every challenge succeeds.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.prompt: An AI service produces 150 deadline claims a day. Policy requires every claim to be reviewed by a person before publication. Reviewers have two hours per day at four minutes per claim. Calculate the daily gap, explain what this means for the control, and propose how to respond.

rubric.text: Reviewers can examine 30 claims a day (120 minutes divided by 4).
The backlog grows by 120 claims a day (150 minus 30).
A control that cannot be performed is not functioning as a control, even if it reads well in the register.
Options include narrowing the feature, such as extracting dates with visible source passages, or adding review capacity.
Publishing unreviewed claims while describing all as reviewed would misstate the control; throughput should be limited to review capacity.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.prompt: After an AI-generated summary is found to be wrong, describe a sound correction sequence: what to do first, how to find and fix copies, how to communicate, and what to keep open.

rubric.text: Pause publication of affected items and preserve evidence, including source identifiers, the output, approvals and publication records.
Identify cause, such as an evaluation that checked citation existence but not support.
Locate and correct copies in systems the team controls; acknowledge copies outside its control as a limitation.
Issue the correction through the same channel that carried the error, and have the approver review the changed process.
Keep the reporting route open in case the correction missed an effect, and record the governance changes made.

questions.source: When deferral is the responsible output
questions.prompt: A company wants to use an LLM to rank employees for promotion. The evaluation cannot observe real career outcomes, employees have not been consulted, the data boundary is unclear and no manager has agreed to own the decisions. Argue for what the team should do, including options other than full deployment, and what to record.

rubric.text: Defer: the preconditions for responsible use are missing (consultation, ownership, a measurable consequential outcome, a known data boundary).
Technical feasibility or a good proxy score is not a reason to proceed.
Narrowing is an option, such as limiting the tool to organizing documents rather than ranking people, or using synthetic data.
Record why the team deferred and what evidence or capacity would justify reconsideration.
A record that can only say "go" is a rubber stamp; stopping or narrowing is a legitimate result.

questions.source: When deferral is the responsible output
questions.prompt: An agent with access to a CRM can send e-mails to customers on its own, and leadership is worried about errors. List four ways to narrow the workflow and explain what each reduces.

rubric.text: Draft for human sending instead of autonomous sending: adds review and reversibility before external effects.
Synthetic or test customer data in pilots: removes exposure of real people.
Shorter retention of traces: reduces privacy exposure over time.
Removing high-impact actions such as refunds until outcome checks exist: limits severe harm.
A disclaimer alone is not a narrowing, because it shifts burden to recipients without reducing risk.

questions.source: When deferral is the responsible output
questions.prompt: A vendor says "a human is in the loop" for a system that produces 500 decisions an hour reviewed by one person clicking Approve. Explain what is missing from the claim and how to specify a meaningful human review step.

rubric.text: "Human in the loop" names a person but not a control: the task, evidence, authority, time budget and stop rule must be defined.
At 500 items an hour (about 7 seconds each) the reviewer cannot meaningfully assess content.
The reviewer needs authority to reject and information needed to judge.
Throughput should be limited to review and response capacity.
Review quality should be measured, for example by seeded errors or sampling, to detect rubber-stamping.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.prompt: Describe four distinct ways a governance record for an AI system can look complete while the system remains ungoverned. Consider the roles the record names, the mitigations it offers, the triggers it sets, and the people it claims to have consulted. Give a one-line concrete example of each.

rubric.text: Roles filled with generic labels (such as "the team") so that no identifiable person has accepted responsibility or holds authority to act.
A mitigation that does not address the stated harm mechanism, for example an answer-accuracy test offered for a risk of stored data being exposed.
A trigger with no observable signal or measurement procedure, such as "act when quality falls", so nobody can tell whether it fired.
Consultation that is simulated or token, such as model-generated stakeholder reactions presented as feedback from people, or a completed form treated as legal clearance.
Gives a concrete example for each and explains why the record looks fine while the system is not governed.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.prompt: A chatbot logs users' health questions for a year. The register lists the harm as exposure of sensitive health information from the retained logs, and the mitigation as a weekly accuracy test of the chatbot's answers. Analyze the mismatch and propose controls that fit the harm.

rubric.text: The accuracy test addresses answer correctness, not exposure of stored data.
A mitigation must match the mechanism of the stated harm.
The accuracy test may be valuable for another risk, but does not reduce this one.
Fitting controls include shortening or eliminating retention, redacting health details before logging, and restricting access to logs.
The register should name an owner and an observable signal, such as audit of access to the logs, for the harm that was actually listed.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.prompt: Explain what it means for a governance register to be a control plane rather than documentation. Give three examples of effects a register entry could have on a running AI system.

rubric.text: A control plane's contents determine what the system is allowed to do; documentation only describes it.
Example: changing an entry pauses execution or removes a tool permission.
Example: revoking an approval stops an action bound to it, or shortening retention triggers deletion.
Example: changing the evaluation requirement blocks release until the new check passes.
If updating the register changes nothing in the system, it is only documentation.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.prompt: Draft the structure of an honest sign-off for a governance record, explaining what each part contains and why the "not checked" part matters. Also say when withholding a signature is the right result.

rubric.text: Checked: which register lines the signer confirmed against the running system and which owners confirmed their roles.
How: the method, such as own tests, exercising the route, inspecting stores, conversation with an owner, or help from an AI assistant and which parts.
Not checked: unverified systems like providers and backups, behavior under real load, consultation not done.
Not claiming: that the workflow is ethical, consented to or compliant, or that "ready for review" means someone reviewed.
Withholding is right when the evidence does not support signing, and the correct action is to narrow or defer the workflow rather than reword the sign-off.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.prompt: An AI-assisted workflow publishes a wrong figure. The user who reported it, the content owner, the vendor of the drafting tool, the provider of the underlying model and the institution that supplied the data all made choices that mattered. Explain how responsibility distributes and what a team should record.

rubric.text: In socio-technical systems each party's choice may be necessary while none is sufficient alone.
Naming one owner does not remove dependencies on the others.
The record should show for each dependency whether it was checked or only assumed.
A useful question is what change made before the incident would have prevented it.
The answer should be an action someone takes, not a sentence someone writes.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.prompt: An organization's policy forbids pasting customer data into public chatbots, yet employees are rewarded for speed and those who raise concerns are called obstructive. Explain why the policy is likely to fail and what changes would make it work.

rubric.text: People do what an organization rewards, not what its documents say.
If speed is rewarded and listening is not, the stated policy and actual behavior diverge.
Authority to pause or object is nominal if exercising it is penalized.
Time and resources for review and consultation must be allocated.
Measures include aligning incentives, protecting those who raise concerns, giving approved tools that fit the work, and monitoring actual practice.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.prompt: A team deploys a coding agent that can read files, run shell commands and call external services in developers' environments. Describe how to reduce its risk through permissions and handling of untrusted input, and how to connect those measures to a governance record.

rubric.text: Apply least privilege: grant only the permissions the task needs and keep the agent out of broader credentials.
Require approval for actions with side effects, and avoid blanket permanent approvals.
Treat text from web pages, documents or tool output as data, because it may contain instructions meant to hijack the agent.
Prefer sandboxing and restricted environments to limit damage.
In the register tie each measure to a named owner, a monitoring signal and an incident response, instead of copying generic security prose.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.prompt: A developer records a decision note for an AI-assisted policy change. Describe what the note should contain, why it separates the model's proposal from human input, and how a reader can tell whether a person actually reviewed it.

rubric.text: It records what the model proposed, what a person added or corrected, the evidence supporting the recommendation, and whose interests are served or disadvantaged.
It ends with a named human recommendation.
Separation shows where a person changed substance and where they merely accepted the draft.
Sentences that simply repeat the model are flagged, since repetition is not review.
Evidence cited should be independent of the model's fluency, and the note should show the person's reasoning.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.prompt: A team announces "We are compliant" after completing an internal AI-use register. Explain why that statement is unsupported, and distinguish the roles of structural checks, legal review and ethical judgment.

rubric.text: A completed internal form is not regulatory approval.
Lawful basis for processing personal data is a legal determination that depends on law, jurisdiction and facts.
Some regulations require specific processes, such as impact assessments, that must actually be carried out.
Legal compliance is not the same as ethical acceptability; lawful practices can still harm people.

Structural checks catch missing information, legal review addresses obligations, and ethical judgment involves affected people and consequences, with each leaving open questions the others cannot answer.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.prompt: A policy says records are deleted "30 days after the case is created". A case was created on 10 January 2027 and last used on 20 February 2027 (not a leap year). Compute the deletion date under creation-based and last-use-based readings, state the difference, and list what a retention policy should specify.

rubric.text: Creation-based: 30 days after 10 January is 9 February 2027.
Last-use-based: 30 days after 20 February is 22 March 2027.
The two interpretations differ by 41 days.
The policy should state when the clock starts, who performs deletion, and how deletion is checked.
It should also cover all copies, including backups, derived data and provider-held data.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.prompt: A company sends customer messages to an external LLM provider's API and records "retention: 0 days" because its own systems store nothing. Critique that entry and say what the company should record instead.

rubric.text: Data sent to the provider is a copy handled under the provider's terms.
The company should read the terms for its service tier and record unknowns instead of assuming zero.
Zero retention in the company's own systems does not establish zero retention elsewhere.
The register should distinguish stores the company inspected from those it relies on others' statements about.
Using a provider does not remove the company's responsibility to its customers for the data it chose to send.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.prompt: A team compares three agent actions: saving a draft in a private workspace, sending an e-mail to external customers, and publishing to an indexed public website. Explain how reversibility and action surface should influence governance, and why model accuracy alone is not enough.

rubric.text: Private drafts can be deleted without others having seen them, so they are the easiest to reverse.
E-mails and public posts escape the team's control once sent; recipients and crawlers keep copies.
Less reversible actions justify stronger review, narrower scope and tighter approval.
A rollback plan limits damage when errors occur, whatever the accuracy.
Equal accuracy across actions does not mean equal consequences, so oversight should scale with the consequences.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.prompt: A developer asks an LLM to critique a register entry, with instructions not to rewrite it and to list group-named owners, thresholds without signals, mitigations that do not address the named harm, and one undocumented decision. Explain why this prompt is better than asking the model to improve the entry, and how to treat the model's findings.

rubric.text: A rewrite tends to smooth over weak lines, hiding vagueness instead of exposing it.
The critique keeps authorship and decisions with the person.
The prompt targets specific known failure patterns, which makes the output checkable.
Each finding should be verified against the entry, since a finding that cannot be located may be a plausible guess.
The absence of findings does not prove the entry is sound.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.prompt: During stakeholder conversations, a student says they care more about being quoted without context than about accuracy, and a maintainer says an appeals channel would create unpaid support work. Explain how such concerns should influence the design and why prepared questionnaires may miss them.

rubric.text: Open-ended listening can reveal concerns outside the categories the designers anticipated.
The student's concern may change data classes, quoting rules or purpose.
The maintainer's workload concern shows a recourse route must be staffed to function.
Concerns should be recorded, with design changes made or the reasons for declining them.
Unresolved concerns should be tracked and, where serious, should constrain the workflow until addressed.

questions.source: A register makes questions inspectable
questions.prompt: A register's roles include owner, approver and incident contact. Explain what each is for, why they should be distinct where possible, and what goes wrong if all three are assigned to one person to complete the form.

rubric.text: The owner is accountable for the workflow as a continuing system.
The approver decides whether a proposal or change goes ahead.
The incident contact is where people report problems and starts the response.
Separate roles provide independent review and cover for absence.
One person in all roles removes independence, creates a single point of failure and may be implicated in the incident.

questions.source: Who decided? Five choices that exist before the form does
questions.prompt: A company argues that because an AI system cannot be sued, no one needs to be accountable for its outputs. Explain why this is wrong, and what accountability for AI-assisted decisions should look like.

rubric.text: An AI system is not a legal person; responsibility falls on natural persons and organizations.
Choosing to deploy and rely on a system is a human decision with consequences.
Someone must be able to answer for outcomes, correct errors and stop the system.
The accountable party should be named and have authority and resources.
A system may stop its own work as a safe default, but this does not move accountability to the system.

questions.source: A register makes questions inspectable
questions.prompt: A hollow governance record has a green validator status but no working response. Describe how a team can test whether its incident route works, and what a failing result would look like.

rubric.text: Send a clearly labeled test report to the named incident contact.
Check whether it is acknowledged within the stated time.
A failing result is no acknowledgment, an unreachable contact, or an acknowledgment with no one able to act.
Test the backup path and the escalation when the first contact is unavailable.
Record the date, the result and any fixes; this upgrades the claim from "a contact is named" to "the route was exercised and worked".

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.prompt: A retention-day validator must accept non-negative integers (including 0) and reject negative numbers, Booleans, strings and floats. Describe two plausible wrong implementations that a good test suite must catch, explain the specific inputs that expose each, and explain why passing only a demonstration case is not enough.

rubric.text: Wrong version one accepts anything that isinstance(int) accepts, so True passes as one day; the test input is True.
Wrong version two treats any falsy value as missing, so a deliberate zero is rejected; the test input is 0.
A demonstration case with a typical value like 30 and an empty record passes under both wrong versions.
Boundary and type cases are needed: zero, negative, Boolean, string and float.
A suite should be checked against deliberately wrong implementations to confirm it can tell right from wrong.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.prompt: A developer's validator tests all pass. State what this establishes and what it does not, and describe two things the developer should do beyond running the tests to understand the result.

rubric.text: The tests establish that the exercised behaviors work as the tests specify.
They do not establish reliability for untested inputs, the adequacy of the specification, or permission to deploy.
The developer should walk through one passing case from input to returned status without relying on an assistant's explanation.
The developer should explain why one raised error belongs to the contract, as refusing invalid input is part of what the validator promises.
The developer should record the commands, outputs and interpretation, and test the strongest claim in the write-up by asking what evidence, and whose action, actually supports it.

questions.source: Tear down the packet validator
questions.prompt: A project submission must contain ten named Markdown files. An automated validator reports `structurally_complete: True` when each file exists inside the submission folder and holds at least forty characters after whitespace is stripped. A student submits ten files that each contain the same sixty-character string of the letter x, and the validator passes them. An empty folder fails with ten "missing" issues. Explain why the pass is expected behavior rather than a bug, what the pair of cases shows about what a mechanical check can and cannot establish, and what a reviewer must do next.

rubric.text: States that the validator tests only existence, location, and length, and the junk files satisfy all three, so the pass is what the specification produces.
Explains that nothing in the files shows a need, a design, an implementation, a test, or a decision, so presence and length are not evidence of substance.
Notes that the empty folder and the junk submission together show the check separates "absent" from "present" but cannot separate "present" from "meaningful."
Says structure can be checked mechanically while substance requires connected evidence and accountable human judgment, and that a stricter length floor would not change this.
States that the reviewer must read the content, test whether each file performs its role and whether the files support one another, and that the validator's output should say what it did not check.

questions.source: Tear down the packet validator
questions.prompt: Design a small validator for a submission of ten required files. Name the checks it should perform and the order you would run them, say what each check can and cannot detect, and write the sentence the validator should return alongside its boolean result. Explain why keeping the validator narrow is a strength.

rubric.text: Names a containment check (resolved path stays inside the submission folder), a presence check (path is a regular file), and a minimum-content check (stripped text length at least some floor).
Gives a sound order, with containment before reading any content so that links to outside files are never opened, and explains why the order matters.
States what each check cannot detect: containment does not judge content safety, presence does not judge relevance, and the length floor catches stubs but not padding or copied text.
Specifies a returned note saying that evidence, authority, and understanding still require human review, and names the boolean something like structurally complete rather than valid or approved.
Argues that narrow checks fail for nameable reasons and cannot be satisfied by fluent prose, whereas relevance heuristics invite gaming, so the narrowness is what makes the result trustworthy.

questions.source: Tear down the packet validator
questions.prompt: A script checks that each required file in a folder lies inside the folder before reading it. A student replaces one required file with a symbolic link to a file elsewhere on the machine. Explain how a well-built containment check catches this, why the path must be resolved before it is compared with the folder, and what a containment check still cannot tell you about the files that pass it.

rubric.text: Explains that the link's own name lies inside the folder, so only the resolved real path reveals that the target is outside.
Describes resolving the path (following links and removing `..` segments) and then comparing path components with the resolved root, for example with a path-aware relative-to test.
Notes that comparing raw strings by prefix is wrong because a sibling directory such as `/srv/work-old` shares the prefix of `/srv/work`.
Explains that the check should run before the file is read so a link cannot cause the validator to open data outside the folder.
States that containment says where a file lives, not whether its contents are true, safe, or free of malicious instructions, so a file inside can still be harmful.

questions.source: Tear down the packet validator
questions.prompt: A team proposes to improve their submission validator by scoring each document for relevance: count how many words from the project goal appear in the document and pass it at 70 percent overlap. The documents are written by an LLM that was given the goal text. Evaluate this proposal. Explain why it is easy to satisfy without achieving the aim, and describe a check that would fail differently from LLM prose, along with that check's limits.

rubric.text: Explains that keyword overlap measures surface vocabulary, and a model prompted with the goal text will naturally echo that vocabulary.
Observes that a check reading only the surface of prose is satisfied best by the thing that produces fluent prose most easily, so the check and the producer fail together.

Proposes a check with a different failure route, such as executing a documented command and comparing its output, tracing a claim to a source passage, or having a person answer a targeted question about the document.
States a limit of the proposed check, for example that it covers only the claims sampled, depends on the quality of the reference, or still needs human judgment about interpretation.
Concludes that raising the threshold or adding more keywords makes gaming slightly harder but does not turn a surface heuristic into a measure of substance.

questions.source: Build a claim-to-evidence graph
questions.prompt: An assistant generates a claim-to-evidence table of 36 links in about a minute; each link states that a particular piece of evidence supports a particular claim. Checking one link means opening the evidence it points to and confirming it supports the claim, which takes a reviewer about 4 minutes. Compute the review time for all links, compare it with generation time, and explain what this asymmetry implies for how a project should plan its work and what it should claim.

rubric.text: Computes 36 links times 4 minutes equals 144 minutes, or 2.4 hours, of checking.
